label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For every $m\in(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^5$ the planar five-body problem with masses $m$ has finitely many central configurations up to similarity.
head: environment

label: lem:realpos
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:realpos}
Let $m\in(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^5$. Every central configuration with masses $m$ is similar, by an orientation-preserving similarity, to exactly two positive normalized central configurations, which differ by the rotation by $\pi$. In particular, if \eqref{eq:AK4} has finitely many solutions, there are finitely many central configurations up to similarity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Taking the scalar product of \eqref{eq:cc} with $m_i(q_i-c)$ and summing gives $\lambda I=U$ with $I=\sum_im_i|q_i-c|^2>0$ and $U=\sum_{i<j}m_im_j/r_{ij}>0$. So $\lambda>0$. We translate $c$ to the origin, scale by $\lambda^{1/3}$, and rotate so that $q_1-q_2$ is horizontal. Exactly two rotations do this. Conversely, the translation and the scale of a positive normalized central configuration are fixed by \eqref{eq:AK4}.
head: environment

label: lem:slice
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (a) The rows $D_{kl}$ are invariant and $Z_k$, $W_k$ are multiplied by $s$, $s^{-1}$. The action is free because $u_1\ne0$ on $X_m$. The inverse of the map is $x\mapsto(u_1,u_1^{-1}\cdot x)$. The point $s\cdot x$ lies in $\{u_{12}=v_{12}\}$ if and only if $s^2=v_{12}/u_{12}$. (b) The rows for $tm$ at the image point are multiples of the rows for $m$. For a relabelling, we translate the new body $5$ to the origin and rotate to restore $u_1=1$. (c) Multiplying the masses by $t$ multiplies the right side of \eqref{eq:cc} by $t^2$ and the left side by $t$ for fixed $\lambda$. Relabelling permutes the equations.
head: environment

label: lem:potential
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:potential}
On $\{D_{kl}=0\}$, with $\nabla_u$ and $\nabla_v$ the gradients in $(u_1,\dots,u_4)$ and $(v_1,\dots,v_4)$,
\[
(Z_1,\dots,Z_4)=2A\,\nabla_vV,\qquad (W_1,\dots,W_4)=2A\,\nabla_uV,\qquad A=\operatorname{diag}(m_1^{-1},\dots,m_4^{-1})+m_5^{-1}\mathbb{1}\mathbb{1}^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The matrix $A$ is invertible, with $A^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(m_1,\dots,m_4)-mm^{\mathsf T}/M$ (restricted to the first four coordinates).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We write $\tilde F_k=\sum_{l\ne k}m_l(u_l-u_k)p_{kl}^3$, so that $Z_k=u_k+\tilde F_k-\tilde F_5$. From $p_{kl}^2u_{kl}v_{kl}=1$ we get $\partial p_{kl}/\partial v_k=-\tfrac12p_{kl}^3u_{kl}$. So $\partial U/\partial v_k=\tfrac12m_k\tilde F_k$. Also $\partial I/\partial v_k=m_k(u_k-u_G)$ with $u_G=\sum_lm_lu_l/M$. Hence $(2/m_k)\,\partial V/\partial v_k=u_k-u_G+\tilde F_k$. By antisymmetry $\sum_{l=1}^5m_l\tilde F_l=0$. Since $u_5=0$, also $\sum_{l\le4}m_l(u_l-u_G)=m_5u_G$. Hence $(2/m_5)\sum_{l\le4}\partial V/\partial v_l=u_G-\tilde F_5$ and $(2A\nabla_vV)_k=u_k+\tilde F_k-\tilde F_5=Z_k$. Exchanging $u$ and $v$ gives the rows $W_k$.

label: lem:U
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:U}
Let $M\ne0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item On $X_m$, $U=\sum_km_kz_kw_k=I$, with $z,w$ recentred at the centre of mass.
\item $U$ is constant on every irreducible component of $X_m$ and of $Y_m$, in particular on every irreducible curve $C\subseteq Y_m$.
\item For $m\in(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^5$, $U=I>0$ at the point of $Y_m$ given by a real central configuration.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (a) In the coordinates $z,w$ of \eqref{eq:AK4} the centre of mass is at the origin and $I=\sum_km_kz_kw_k$. We multiply the equation for $z_k$ by $m_kw_k$ and sum over $k$. By antisymmetry and $p_{kl}^2z_{kl}w_{kl}=1$, $\sum_km_kz_kw_k=\sum_{k<l}m_km_lp_{kl}^3z_{kl}w_{kl}=\sum_{k<l}m_km_lp_{kl}=U$. (b) By Lemma~\ref{lem:potential} and the invertibility of $A$, the gradient of $V$ on $\{D_{kl}=0\}$ vanishes at every point of $X_m$. The differential of $V$ therefore vanishes on the tangent space of each irreducible component at its smooth points, which form a connected dense open subset. Hence $V$ is constant on the component. By (a), $V=\tfrac32U$ on $X_m$. (c) is the identity $\lambda I=U$ of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:realpos}, with $\lambda=1$.
head: environment

label: cor:U
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:U}
Let $m\in(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^5$. If $Y_m$ contains no irreducible curve on which some $r_{kl}^2$ is non-constant and $U$ is not identically zero, then the planar five-body problem with masses $m$ has finitely many central configurations up to similarity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Infinitely many central configurations give infinitely many points of $Y_m$ with $U>0$ (Lemmas~\ref{lem:realpos}, \ref{lem:slice} and \ref{lem:U}(c)), hence an irreducible curve $C\subseteq Y_m$ on which $U$ is a positive constant. The fibres of $(u,v,p)\mapsto(r_{kl}^2)_{k<l}$ on $Y_m$ have at most $2^{13}$ points (fix the distances: $u_1=1$ determines $v_1$, each $u_k$ is a root of a quadratic, and the signs of the $p_{kl}$ are free). Hence some $r_{kl}^2$ is not constant on $C$.

label: lem:orders
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orders}
For every pair $kl$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(O\arabic*)}]
\item $\zeta_{kl},\omega_{kl}\ge-2$, $\zeta_{kl}+3\omega_{kl}\le4$ and $3\zeta_{kl}+\omega_{kl}\le4$. Hence $\zeta_{kl},\omega_{kl}\le2$ and $-2\le x_{kl}\le1$.
\item There is a $z$-stroke $kl$ if and only if $\zeta_{kl}+3\omega_{kl}=4$, and a $w$-stroke if and only if $3\zeta_{kl}+\omega_{kl}=4$.
\item On a $z$-stroke, $\zeta_{kl}=3x_{kl}-2$, $\omega_{kl}=2-x_{kl}$ and $0\le x_{kl}\le1$. On a $w$-stroke, $\omega_{kl}=3x_{kl}-2$ and $\zeta_{kl}=2-x_{kl}$.
\item $x_{kl}=1$ if and only if $kl$ is a $zw$-edge. A $z$-stroke is maximal \textup{(}its ends are not $z$-close, \cite[Def.~6]{AK12}\textup{)} if and only if $x_{kl}=0$.
\item In every triangle $klm$ the minimum of $\zeta_{kl},\zeta_{lm},\zeta_{mk}$ is attained at least twice, and the same holds for $\omega$.
\item If $k$ is $z$-circled and $l$ is not, then $\zeta_{kl}=-2$. If $\zeta_{kl}=2$, then $\omega_{kl}=-2$ and $kl$ is a $w$-stroke.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (O1) Since $e(z_k)\ge-2$ for all $k$, $\zeta_{kl}\ge\min(e(z_k),e(z_l))\ge-2$. The two linear inequalities are $e(Z_{kl})\ge-2$ and $e(W_{kl})\ge-2$. (O2) A stroke means $e(Z_{kl})=-2$. (O3) We solve $\zeta+3\omega=4$, $\zeta+\omega=2x$, and use $\zeta\ge-2$. (O4) If $\zeta+\omega=2$, the inequalities of (O1) give $\zeta\le1$ and $\omega\le1$, hence $\zeta=\omega=1$ and both strokes are present. Conversely a $zw$-edge has $\zeta=\omega=1$. A $z$-stroke has $z$-close ends if and only if $\zeta>-2$, i.e.\ $x>0$. (O5) follows from $z_{kl}+z_{lm}+z_{mk}=0$. (O6) $e(z_k)=-2<e(z_l)$ gives $\zeta_{kl}=-2$. If $\zeta_{kl}=2$, (O1) gives $\omega_{kl}\le-2$, hence $\omega_{kl}=-2$ and $3\zeta_{kl}+\omega_{kl}=4$.

label: lem:S1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:S1}
At a place with diagram $1$, $\mu_t=3a-2$ for every $t\in T$. At a place with diagram $4$, $\mu_t=1$ for every $t\in T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Diagram 1. In the second pattern $w_{1t_0}\prec w_{1t}$ for the body $t_0$ with the larger exponent and both other $t\in T$. Since $12$ is the only maximal $z$-edge, the $z$-diagram is $\{12\}$, an isolated component, and $m_1^3+m_2^3>0$, Proposition~4 of \cite{AK12} excludes this. Suppose all $\mu_t$ equal $\mu<3a-2$. Then we have:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\omega_{12}=2$ by (O3);
\item $\mu<2$, since $\mu=2$ would make $1t$ a $z$-stroke by (O2);
\item $\zeta_{12}=\zeta_{t2}=-2$ by (O6).
\end{enumerate} Proposition~1 of \cite{AK12} with the colours exchanged then gives $e(w_1),e(w_2)\ge2$. The differences $w_{1t}-w_{1t'}=\pm w_{tt'}$ have exponent $3a-2>\mu$. Consequently $w_{13}$, $w_{14}$, $w_{15}$ have the same coefficient $\kappa\ne0$ at exponent $\mu$. As $w_t=w_1-w_{1t}$ and $e(w_1)\ge2>\mu$, the coefficient of $m_3w_3+m_4w_4+m_5w_5$ at exponent $\mu$ is $-(m_3+m_4+m_5)\kappa\ne0$. But this sum equals $-(m_1w_1+m_2w_2)$, whose exponent is at least $2$. Hence $\mu_t=3a-2$ for all $t$.

Diagram 4 is the same argument with $3a-2$ replaced by $1$: the $z$-strokes of the triangle $T$ have $x=1$ and are not maximal. Again $12$ is the only maximal $z$-edge and an isolated component.

label: lem:zwK4
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Inside $Q$, $e(z_{il})=e(w_{il})=1$ for each pair by (O4). If $\alpha_i<\frac12$ for some $i$, then $z_{i'j}=z_{i'i}+z_{ij}$ gives $\alpha_{i'}=\alpha_i$ for all $i'\in Q$. Otherwise all $\alpha_i\ge\frac12$. Two indices with $\alpha_k,\alpha_{k'}>\frac12$ would give $e(z_{kk'})>1$. Either all $\alpha_i$ equal some $\alpha\le\frac12$, or exactly one exceeds $\frac12$ and the others equal $\frac12$. The same holds for the $\beta_i$.
(2) Not both colours have an exceptional index: $\alpha_k>\frac12$ and $\beta_{k'}>\frac12$ give $x_{k'j}>1$, against (O1).
(3) No exceptional index. Then $x_{ij}=\alpha+\beta=c$ for all $i$. By (O4), $c<1$. After exchanging colours we may assume $\alpha<\frac12$. We fix $k\in Q$. The sum $\sum_{i\in Q}m_iz_{ij}=M_Qz_{kj}+\sum_{i\in Q}m_iz_{ik}$ has exponent $2\alpha$, as the second sum has exponent at least $1>2\alpha$ and $M_Q\ne0$. The centre of mass gives $\sum_{i\in Q}m_iz_i-M_Qz_j=-Mz_j$, whence $e(z_j)=2\alpha$. The first equation of \eqref{eq:AK4} for $j$ reads $z_j=\sum_{i\in Q}m_iZ_{ji}$ with $e(Z_{ji})=2\alpha-3c$, which forces $2\alpha\ge2\alpha-3c$, i.e.\ $c\ge0$. Since $\alpha=c-\beta\ge c-\frac12$, $e(Z_{ij})=2\alpha-3c\ge-1-c>-2$, and likewise $e(W_{ij})>-2$: no stroke meets $j$.
(4) An exceptional index $k$ in $z$. By (2) all $\beta_i$ equal some $\beta$. We have $\beta<\frac12$, since otherwise $x_{ij}=1$ for $i\ne k$. Hence $x_{kj}=\frac a2+\beta$ and $x_{ij}=\frac12+\beta$. As in (3), $e(w_j)=2\beta$. The second equation of \eqref{eq:AK4} for $j$ reads $w_j=\sum_{i\in Q}m_iW_{ji}$, with $e(W_{ji})=2\beta-3x_{ij}$, which is $-\frac32-\beta$ for $i\ne k$ and $-\frac32a-\beta$ for $i=k$. Since $a>1$ the term $i=k$ has the strictly smallest exponent. So $2\beta=e(w_j)=-\frac32a-\beta$, i.e.\ $\beta=-\frac a2$. Then $x_{kj}=0$ and $x_{ij}=\frac{1-a}2$. Now $e(W_{kj})=-a\ge-2$ gives $a\le2$, with equality if and only if $kj$ is a $w$-stroke. The other exponents $e(Z_{kj})=a$, $e(Z_{ij})=1+\frac32(a-1)$ and $e(W_{ij})=\frac{a-3}2$ exceed $-2$. If $a=2$, then $\omega_{kj}=-2$: $k$ and $j$ are not $w$-close, and the $w$-stroke $kj$ is maximal. In that case $kj$ is a $w$-edge, since $e(Z_{kj})=a=2>-2$.

label: lem:infty
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:infty}
Let $P$ be a place of diagram $5$ at a mass at which one of the models of this subsection is valid, and let $o$ be the vector of the orders at $P$ of the modelled quantities, with $o_v=+\infty$ when the quantity vanishes identically along $C$. Then the model has a point with real coordinates whose projection to the five coordinates of the type equals that of $o$. In particular the type of $P$ lies in the hull of the model.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Each relation of a model that requires a minimum to be attained twice comes from an exact linear identity, with nonzero constant coefficients, among the modelled quantities, such as $m_Az_A+m_Bz_B+M_Tz_c=0$ for the centre of mass $z_c$ of $T$. It still holds when the terms that vanish identically are dropped. The quantities that can vanish identically are the positions $z_A$, $z_B$, $z_c$, $w_A$, $w_B$, $w_c$, the differences $z_X-z_c$ for a body in mode Z1 or Zs and $w_X-w_c$ for one in mode W1 or Ws, the sums $\sum_tm_tZ_{tX}$ of the bodies in modes Z1 and W1 and, for $V_2^{\mathrm w}$, in mode F, the two torques, the quantities of (R3), and $1-Mp_{AB}^3$. Each of them enters the relations only in lower bounds, in the equality of the orders of the two torques, which vanish together, with coefficient $+1$ in the terms of a minimum, or in upper bounds that are switched off by the event of (R1), (R2) or (R3) triggered by its vanishing. We replace every infinite order by a number $L$ larger than $10+3\max|o_v|$, the maximum over the finite orders. We use $L+2$ for $1-Mp_{AB}^3$, and $L+1$ for the two quantities of (R3) when all terms of that relation are infinite. The lower bounds and the equality of the torques then hold. The upper bounds that are not switched off involve only finite orders. A term of a minimum that contains a replaced order is at least $L-2$. All other terms are at most $3\max|o_v|+2$. Hence a minimum attained twice by finite terms keeps its value and the pair attaining it. The three relations whose terms can all be infinite hold with the values chosen. Since the projection involves only finite orders, it is unchanged. By Theorem~\ref{thm:hulls}, it lies in the hull.

label: lem:X
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:X}
If \textup{(35)}$_A$ holds and $4a'+3b'\le4$, then $\mathsf{R}(cd;s)$. Symmetrically, if \textup{(35)}$_B$ holds and $3a'+4b'\le4$, then $\mathsf{R}(ab;s)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We put $C_w=\sum_{k\in\{a,b\},\,l\in\{c,d\}}m_km_lW_{kl}$. From the equations $w_k=\sum_{l\ne k}m_lW_{kl}$ of $a$ and $b$ in \eqref{eq:AK4}, $m_aw_a+m_bw_b=m_sA_w+C_w$. With $w_a=w_s+w_{as}$ and $w_b=w_s+w_{bs}$ this becomes
\[
(m_a+m_b)\,w_s=m_sA_w+C_w-m_aw_{as}-m_bw_{bs}.
\]
We compare each term with $w_{cd}$, of exponent $3b'-2$. The three pairs of $A$ have the same $(\zeta,\omega)$. So $W_{as}$, $W_{bs}$ and $W_{ab}$ have the same exponent $2-4a'$. Under (35)$_A$ the two terms of $A_w$ cancel at leading order and $e(A_w)>2-4a'\ge3b'-2$ on or below $\mathrm{LA}$. The cross terms have $e(C_w)\ge4-\frac92a'-\frac32b'$, which exceeds $3b'-2$ because $a'+b'<\frac43$ on or below $\mathrm{LA}$. And $e(w_{as})=2-a'>3b'-2$ as $a',b'<1$. Hence $w_s\prec w_{cd}$. By the centre of mass, $M w_s=m_cw_{sc}+m_dw_{sd}+m_aw_{sa}+m_bw_{sb}$, which gives $m_cw_{sc}+m_dw_{sd}\prec w_{cd}$: the body $s$ is at the $w$-centre of mass of $\{c,d,s\}$ at the scale $w_{cd}$. The reduction of \cite[pp.~577--578]{AK12} uses exactly this relation, the equations of $c$ and $d$ at exponent $-2$ (in which only the two stroke terms survive, because $w_k-w_G$ has exponent at least $3b'-2>-2$ and the cross terms have exponent $4-\frac92a'-\frac32b'>-2$), the closure of the triangle $cds$ in both colours with $p^2zw=1$ on its pairs, and the positivity of $m_c,m_d,m_s$. Eliminating the leading coefficients from this system, we obtain $\mathsf{R}(cd;s)$ times a factor that is positive on $(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^3$. Hence $\mathsf{R}(cd;s)$.

label: def:piece
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:piece}
A \emph{piece} is a polytope $\Pi\subset\mathbb{R}^{10}$ (a point, a segment or a polygon, given by its vertices) together with a set of its faces, the \emph{attained} faces, closed under passing to larger faces. Its \emph{attained set} is the union of the relative interiors of its attained faces. For a set $S$ of labels, $\mathrm{pieces}(S)$ is the list of pieces in Table~\ref{tab:pieces} whose enabling condition is implied by $S$, together with the attained faces of the hull $V_2^{\mathrm w}$ of \S\ref{ss:d5}, or of another hull of \S\ref{ss:d5} where this is stated, embedded for each labelling of diagram~$5$ with $\mathsf{E}(T)\in S$.

label: thm:types
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:types}
Let $m\in(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^5$, let $C\subseteq Y_m$ be an irreducible curve on which some $r_{kl}^2$ is not constant and $U\not\equiv0$, and let $P$ be a singular place of $C$ with diagram $d$ and labelling $\lambda$. Then $x(P)$ lies in the attained set of a piece of $\mathrm{pieces}(S(m))$ of diagram $d$ and labelling $\lambda$. For $d=5$ it lies in the relative interior of an attained face of $V_2^{\mathrm w}$ with that labelling, and of $V_2$ if $m_o\ne m_a+m_b$ for every $o$ in the triangle $T=\{o,a,b\}$ of the place.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{lem:place} the place gives singular sequences with diagram $d$. Hence the conditions of \cite[\S8]{AK12} hold at $m$ for the labelling $\lambda$. These are (23) for diagrams $1$, $4$ and $5$, (29) for $3$, sharpened by Theorem~\ref{thm:D3}, (32) for $6$, the conditions of \S8.7 for $7$, (36) for $10$, and (40) for $8$ and $11$--$13$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:types}, Lemmas~\ref{lem:S1}, \ref{lem:zwK4} and \ref{lem:cut}, and Table~\ref{tab:d7} for diagram $7$, the type lies in the set listed in Table~\ref{tab:types}. This set lies in the attained set of the corresponding piece of Table~\ref{tab:pieces} once its condition holds. Diagram $5$ is treated in \S\ref{ss:d5}, with Lemma~\ref{lem:infty}. Renaming the bodies maps singular places, types, label sets and pieces equivariantly, since all of them are defined through labelled sets of bodies. So it suffices to consider the numbering of \cite[Fig.~11]{AK12}. There the type set of each diagram other than $5$ and $7$ is the attained set of its pieces (compare Tables~\ref{tab:types} and~\ref{tab:pieces} row by row). For diagram~$7$ the attained set of the pieces $\mathsf{d7}(A|B)$ of $\mathrm{pieces}(S)$ is the set of cells allowed for $S$ by the wing rules, which is Table~\ref{tab:d7}.

label: thm:Kgating
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Kgating}
Let $P$ be a singular place of $C$, $j$ a body, $Q=Q_j$, $k\in Q$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item If $x(P)\in\{\mathsf{u}_0(j)\}\cup\bigcup_{k'}\sigma_{k'}(j)\big((0,1)\big)$, in particular if it lies in the attained set of $\mathsf{d14a}(j)$ or of some $\mathsf{d14b}(j,k')$, then $\mathrm{K14}(m_Q)$ has a solution, formed by the leading coefficients of the cluster at $P$.
\item If $x(P)=\mathsf{b}_k(j)$, then $\mathrm{K15}(m_Q,k)$ has a solution, formed by the leading coefficients of the cluster at $P$.
\item In case \textup{(a)}, $P$ has diagram $14$ with isolated body $j$. In case \textup{(b)}, $P$ has diagram $15$ with isolated body $j$ and $w$-edge $kj$, up to exchanging the colours.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since every listed point has $x=1$ exactly on $\mathrm{tri}(Q_j)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:zwK4} applies. The point $\mathsf{u}_0(j)$ is case (A), $\sigma_{k'}(j)(t)$ with $0<t<1$ is case (B) with $a=1+t<2$, and $\mathsf{b}_k(j)$ is case (B) with $a=2$. This gives (c). Fix $i_0\in Q$ and, for $i,l\in Q$, let $\hat z_i$, $\hat w_i$ and $\hat p_{il}$ be the coefficients of $u_{ii_0}$, $v_{ii_0}$ at exponent $1$ and of $p_{il}$ at exponent $-1$ (in the expansion of Lemma~\ref{lem:place}). For $i\ne l$ in $Q$ these are nonzero and the row $D_{il}$ gives $\hat p_{il}^2\hat z_{il}\hat w_{il}=1$. The first equation of \eqref{eq:AK4} for $i\in Q$ is $z_i=\sum_{l\in Q\setminus i}m_lp_{il}^3z_{il}+m_jZ_{ij}$. Each term of the sum has exponent $-2$ with coefficient $m_l\hat p_{il}^3\hat z_{il}$. The coefficient $c_z$ of $z_i$ at exponent $-2$ does not depend on $i$, since $e(z_{il})=1$. So
\[
F^z_i(\hat z,\hat p)=c_z-m_j[Z_{ij}]_{-2}\qquad(i\in Q),
\]
where $[\,\cdot\,]_{-2}$ is the coefficient at exponent $-2$, nonzero if and only if $ij$ is a $z$-stroke. The same holds for $w$. When we multiply by $m_i$ and sum over $Q$, the left side cancels by antisymmetry. If no $z$-stroke meets $j$, this gives $M_Qc_z=0$ and hence $F^z(\hat z,\hat p)=0$, and likewise for $w$. In case (A) and in case (B) with $a<2$ no stroke meets $j$ and the leading coefficients solve K14$(m_Q)$. label: lem:lex

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose that $0=\sum_{s=1}^N\lambda_sx_s$ with $N\ge1$, $\lambda_s>0$ and $x_s\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(G_{j(s)})$, and let $i$ be the least index such that $j(s)\in I_i$ for some $s$. Each $x_s$ is a convex combination of points of $G_{j(s)}$ with $j(s)\in I_i\cup\dots\cup I_r$. So $l_i\cdot x_s\ge0$ by (i). A point $x$ of $\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(G)$ is a convex combination of all points of $G$ with positive weights: if $b$ is the barycentre of $G$ and $\delta>0$ is so small that $x+\delta(x-b)\in\operatorname{conv}(G)$, then $x=(1+\delta)^{-1}\big(x+\delta(x-b)\big)+\delta(1+\delta)^{-1}b$. Hence (ii) gives $l_i\cdot x_s>0$ whenever $j(s)\in I_i$. There is such an $s$. Therefore we obtain $0=l_i\cdot\sum_s\lambda_sx_s>0$, a contradiction.

label: def:cert
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cert}
Let $S$ be a set of labels and $V$ a D5 hull. Let $\mathcal{A}_V(S)$ be the list of the attained faces of the pieces of $\mathrm{pieces}(S)$ (Definition~\ref{def:piece}), with the attained faces of $V$ in place of those of $V_2^{\mathrm w}$. We record each face by the finite set of its vertices. A \emph{certificate} for $S$ relative to $V$ is a finite sequence $l_1,\dots,l_r\in\mathbb{Z}^{10}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item for each $i$, $l_i\cdot v\ge0$ for every vertex $v$ of every face of $\mathcal{A}_V(S)$ on whose vertices $l_1,\dots,l_{i-1}$ all vanish, and
\item every face of $\mathcal{A}_V(S)$ has a vertex $v$ with $l_i\cdot v>0$ for some $i$.
\end{enumerate}
A set $S$ is \emph{certified} relative to $V$ if it has a certificate relative to $V$.

title: Proof
body_md: Let $C\subseteq Y_m$ be a nontrivial curve. By \eqref{eq:balx} we have $\sum_Pd_Px(P)=0$, with $d_P>0$ and at least one singular place $P$. Thus $0$ is a positive combination of points of $\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal{A}_V(S)}\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(G)$, which is excluded by Lemma~\ref{lem:lex}, applied with the partition $(I_i)$ of the certificate. title: Proof
body_md:
After a normalization we reduce the equations to four polynomials in $\nu^2$ and two further unknowns, eliminate $\nu^2$, take resultants in one of the two unknowns, and show that the resulting polynomials in the other have no common root except $0$ and $1$. Exchanging bodies $2$ and $3$ reduces the second case to the first. We normalize $z=(1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2,0)$ by the symmetries of K15. Momentum gives $3c+\nu(c+d)=0$, so that $c\ne0$. We take $c=1$ by the remaining scaling. Let $s_j$ be the coordinate $p$ of the side opposite body $j\le3$ and $r_j=p_{j4}$, write $s_j=\sigma_0+\sigma_1\mathrm{j}^{j-1}+\sigma_2\mathrm{j}^{1-j}$, and put $k=3\nu^2$, $x=\sigma_1$ and $P=\sigma_0\sigma_2$. With $w_{il}=1/(p_{il}^2z_{il})$, the rows $F^w$ give $\nu r_j=-\sigma_0+\mathrm{j}^{j-1}+\sigma_2\mathrm{j}^{1-j}$. The rows $F^z$ then become three polynomial equations $Z_0,Z_1,Z_2$ in $(\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\sigma_2,k)$. The closure of the triangles in $w$ gives three more, $C_0,C_1,C_2$. We use $Z_0$, $Z_1$, $Z_2$, $C_0$ and $C_1$. Since $\prod_js_j\ne0$, they force $P\ne0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item With $t=\sigma_2$, $Z_2=(P^2-P+t^3)/t$. Hence $t^3=P(1-P)$ and $P\ne1$.
\item Modulo $t^3=P(1-P)$, the equations $Z_1$, $C_1$, $Z_0$ and $C_0$ are, up to sign, products of powers of $t$ and $P$ with
\[
Q-kK,\quad (1-P)(x^4+3P^2)-2PQx,\quad 1-6P+3P^2+P^3+k\big(PQ+(1-P)x^3+6P(1-P)x\big)
\]
and with a polynomial $C_0'$ of degree $1$ in $k$ $(\dagger)$, where $Q=P^2-P+1$ and $K=(1-P)x^2+Px+P(1-P)$. We call the three displayed polynomials (I), (II) and (III). A solution therefore gives $(P,x,k)$ with $P\notin\{0,1\}$ at which (I), (II), (III) and $C_0'$ vanish.
\item Write (III) $=A_3+kB_3$ and $C_0'=A_0+kB_0$ with $A_3,B_3,A_0,B_0$ free of $k$. Put $G_3=KA_3+QB_3$ and $G_0=KA_0+QB_0$. Since (I) is $Q-kK$, we have $G_3=K\cdot\mathrm{(III)}+B_3\cdot\mathrm{(I)}$ and $G_0=K\,C_0'+B_0\cdot\mathrm{(I)}$ $(\dagger)$, so that $G_3$ and $G_0$ vanish at $(P,x)$. The resultants with (II) factor as
\[
\mathrm{Res}_x(\mathrm{II},G_3)=P^3(P-1)^2H_{18}(P),\qquad\mathrm{Res}_x(\mathrm{II},G_0)=27P^6(P-1)^5(P^2-3P+1)^4H_{32}(P),
\]
where $H_{18}$ and $H_{32}$ are irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, of degrees $18$ and $32$, with leading coefficients $5$ and $100$ $(\dagger)$. Since $P\notin\{0,1\}$, $H_{18}(P)=0$ and $(P^2-3P+1)H_{32}(P)=0$. But $H_{18}\equiv1735830-4544451P$ modulo $P^2-3P+1$, a nonzero polynomial with a rational root, while the roots of $P^2-3P+1$ are irrational. Thus $H_{18}$ and $P^2-3P+1$ have no common root. Since $7$ divides neither leading coefficient and the Euclidean algorithm for $H_{32}$ and $H_{18}$ modulo $7$ ends in a nonzero constant, $H_{18}$ and $H_{32}$ have no common root either. Hence no such $P$ exists.
\end{enumerate}
The polynomials and the table of the Euclidean algorithm, which has $19$ rows, are in the supplementary material.

label: prop:P11
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:P11}
Let $m_a,m_b,m_c>0$. There is no $x\in(\mathbb{C}^*)^3$ with $\sum m_ix_i=\sum m_ix_i^3=\sum m_ix_i^{-2}=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We say that three directions in $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ \emph{surround} $0$ if they do not lie in a closed half-circle, that is, if each of the three cyclic gaps between them is less than $\pi$. We use two facts.

(A) Let $w_1,w_2,w_3\in\mathbb{C}^*$ and $\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3>0$ with $\sum\mu_iw_i=0$. Then the arguments of the $w_i$ surround $0$, or all $w_i$ lie on one line through $0$. Indeed, if the arguments do not surround $0$, all $w_i$ lie in a closed half-plane $\{\mathrm{Re}(\bar uz)\ge0\}$ with $|u|=1$. Then $0=\sum\mu_i\mathrm{Re}(\bar uw_i)$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so that all $w_i$ lie on the line $iu\mathbb{R}$.

(B) There are no $\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3$ such that each of the sets $\{\theta_i\}$, $\{2\theta_i\}$ and $\{3\theta_i\}$ surrounds $0$. Indeed, the three conditions are unchanged by a common shift of the $\theta_i$ and by relabelling. If $\{\theta_i\}$ surrounds $0$, we may therefore take $\theta=(0,\pi-s,\pi+t)$ with $s,t>0$ and $s+t<\pi$, so that the gaps are $\pi-s$, $s+t$ and $\pi-t$. Then $2\theta\equiv(0,-2s,2t)$, with gaps $2t$, $2\pi-2s-2t$ and $2s$. The set $\{2\theta_i\}$ surrounds $0$ exactly when $s<\frac\pi2$, $t<\frac\pi2$ and $s+t>\frac\pi2$. Assume this. Then $3s,3t\in(0,\frac{3\pi}2)$. After a rotation by $\pi$ the set $\{3\theta_i\}$ is $\{\pi,-3s,3t\}$. If $3s<\pi$ and $3t<\pi$, its gaps are $\pi-3t$, $\pi-3s$ and $3s+3t>\frac{3\pi}2$. If $3t\ge\pi>3s$, it lies in $[\pi,2\pi]$. If $3s\ge\pi>3t$, it lies in $[0,\pi]$. If $3s\ge\pi$ and $3t\ge\pi$, it lies in $[\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}2]$. In no case does it surround $0$.

Now let $x$ be a solution, and put $\theta_i=\arg x_i$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item $\{\theta_i\}$ surrounds $0$. This is (A) with $w=x$: if all $x_i$ lay on a line through $0$, then $x_i=\lambda r_i$ with $r_i\in\mathbb{R}^*$, and $\sum m_ix_i^{-2}=\lambda^{-2}\sum m_ir_i^{-2}\ne0$.
\item $\{2\theta_i\}$ surrounds $0$. This is (A) with $w=x^{-2}$, whose arguments are the $-2\theta_i$ (a set surrounds $0$ if and only if its mirror image does): if all $x_i^{-2}$ lay on a line through $0$, the $\theta_i$ would lie among four directions at right angles, and three of these lie in a closed half-circle, against (1).
\item $\{3\theta_i\}$ surrounds $0$. This is (A) with $w=x^3$: if all $x_i^3$ lay on a line through $0$, then $\theta_i=\psi+n_i\frac\pi3$ with $n_i\in\mathbb{Z}/6$. By (1) the cyclic gaps between the $n_i$ are less than $3$. As they are also positive with sum $6$, they all equal $2$. So the $n_i$ have the same parity, all $x_i^3$ lie on one ray, and $\sum m_ix_i^3\ne0$.
\end{enumerate}
Steps (1)--(3) contradict (B).

label: prop:G1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:G1}
Let $(\hat z,\hat w)$ solve $\mathrm{K15}(m_Q,k)$ with body $k$ at the origin, where $m_a$, $m_b$, $m_c$, $m_k$ and $M_{Q'}=m_a+m_b+m_c$ are nonzero, and suppose that $\operatorname{rank} L_q\le1$ and $\operatorname{rank} L_{q\varrho}\le1$. Then $(m_k/M_{Q'})^2=-1/s^3$ for a number $s$ with $s^3=\pm3\sqrt{-3}$. In particular $m_k/M_{Q'}$ is not real, and the masses are not all positive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the rank conditions to write $q_{il}$ and $\varrho_{il}$ as products of factors attached to~$i$ and to~$l$, deduce from the rows $D_{il}$ that the three points $1/\hat z_i$ form an equilateral triangle, and compute $s$ and $(m_k/M_{Q'})^2$ from this triangle.

(1) Since $L_q\hat w=c\tilde m\ne0$, $\operatorname{rank} L_q=1$ and $L_q=\sigma vv^{\mathsf T}$. Then $\sigma v(v\cdot\hat w)=c\tilde m$ gives $L_q=\sigma\tilde m\tilde m^{\mathsf T}$ with $\sigma\ne0$. Reading off the entries, we obtain $q_{il}=-\sigma m'_im'_l$ on all six pairs, where $m'=(m_a,m_b,m_c,-M_{Q'})$. Thus $p_{il}^3=-\sigma$ on the outer pairs and $p_{ik}^3=\sigma M_{Q'}/m_k$. The off-diagonal entries $-q_{il}\varrho_{il}$ of $L_{q\varrho}$ are nonzero. Hence $L_{q\varrho}=\sigma'v'v'^{\mathsf T}$ with $\sigma'\ne0$, and in the same way $q_{il}\varrho_{il}=-\sigma'\tilde v_i\tilde v_l$ with $\tilde v=(v'_a,v'_b,v'_c,-v'_a-v'_b-v'_c)$, all of whose entries are nonzero. Hence $\varrho_{il}=\gamma\beta_i\beta_l$ on all six pairs, with $\gamma=\sigma'/\sigma$ and $\beta_i=\tilde v_i/m'_i\ne0$.

(2) We put $\psi_i=1/\hat z_i$. On the pairs through $k$, $\hat z_i=\gamma\beta_i\beta_k\hat w_i$. Inserting this into $\varrho_{il}=\gamma\beta_i\beta_l$ on the outer pairs gives $(1-\beta_i/\beta_k)\psi_i=(1-\beta_l/\beta_k)\psi_l$. If $\beta_i=\beta_k$ for one $i$, all the $\beta$ are equal, $\varrho$ is constant and $\hat w$ is a multiple of $\hat z$, which is excluded. So the common value $\psi_0$ is nonzero, $\beta_i=\beta_k(\psi_i-\psi_0)/\psi_i$, and $1/\hat w_i=\gamma\beta_i\beta_k\psi_i=A(\psi_i-\psi_0)$ with $A=\gamma\beta_k^2$.

(3) Since the $p_{ik}^3$ are equal, $p_{ik}=\varepsilon_i\pi_1$ with $\varepsilon_i^3=1$. The rows $D_{ik}$, $p_{ik}^2\hat z_i\hat w_i=1$, then read $\psi_i(\psi_i-\psi_0)=\varkappa\varepsilon_i^2$ with $\varkappa=\pi_1^2/A$.

(4) Likewise $p_{il}=\varepsilon_{il}\pi_0$ on the outer pairs. As $\hat z_{il}\hat w_{il}=(\psi_i-\psi_l)^2/\big(A\psi_i\psi_l(\psi_i-\psi_0)(\psi_l-\psi_0)\big)$, the rows $D_{il}$ read $(\psi_i-\psi_l)^2=\varepsilon_{il}\varepsilon_i^2\varepsilon_l^2\,\varkappa/\lambda$ with $\lambda=\pi_0^2/\pi_1^2$. So the squared sides of the triangle $\psi_a,\psi_b,\psi_c$ agree up to cube roots of unity: $\theta=(\psi_c-\psi_a)/(\psi_b-\psi_a)$ satisfies $\theta^6=(\theta-1)^6=1$ with $\theta\ne0,1$, whence $|\theta|=|\theta-1|=1$ and $\theta=e^{\pm i\pi/3}$. The triangle is equilateral: $\psi_i=h+R\varpi_i$ with $\{\varpi_a,\varpi_b,\varpi_c\}=\{1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2\}$ and $R\ne0$.

(5) The polynomial $\Phi(\varpi)=(h+R\varpi)(h+R\varpi-\psi_0)=R^2\varpi^2+R(2h-\psi_0)\varpi+h(h-\psi_0)$ takes the values $\Phi(\varpi_i)=\varkappa\varepsilon_i^2$. Hence $R^2=\frac13\sum_i\Phi(\varpi_i)\varpi_i=\varkappa s/3$ with $s=\sum_i\varepsilon_i^2\varpi_i$, a sum of three cube roots of unity. If the three terms are distinct, $s=0$ and $R=0$, which is excluded. If they are all equal to some $\alpha$, then $\Phi(\varpi)=\varkappa\alpha\varpi^2$ at three points and hence identically, so $R(2h-\psi_0)=h(h-\psi_0)=0$, which forces $\psi_0=0$, excluded. So exactly two terms are equal and $s^3=\pm3\sqrt{-3}$.

(6) By (4), $\lambda^3=\varkappa^3/(\psi_b-\psi_a)^6$, and $(\psi_b-\psi_a)^2=R^2(\varpi_b-\varpi_a)^2=-3R^2\varpi_a\varpi_b$, so that $(\psi_b-\psi_a)^6=-27R^6=-\varkappa^3s^3$ and $\lambda^3=-1/s^3$.

(7) We choose $\pi_0=p_{ab}$ and $\pi_1=p_{ak}$. Then (1) gives $(\pi_0/\pi_1)^3=-m_k/M_{Q'}$. So $(m_k/M_{Q'})^2=\lambda^3=-1/s^3$, a nonzero imaginary number.

body_md:
\label{lem:G2mass}
For any four points $(z_i,w_i)$, $i\in Q$, with $(z_k,w_k)=(0,0)$ and distinct $z_i$, and with $\tilde u$ and $S_i$ formed from them as above, $\sum_{i\in Q}\tilde u_iS_iz_i^j=0$ for $j=0,1,2$. In case (ii), therefore, $\sum_{i\in Q'}m_i\hat z_i^2=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: When we group the double sum by pairs, the pair $\{i,l\}$ contributes $\tilde u_i\tilde u_lw_{il}^2(z_i^j-z_l^j)/(z_i-z_l)$, that is $0$, $\tilde u_i\tilde u_lw_{il}^2$ and $\tilde u_i\tilde u_lw_{il}^2(z_i+z_l)$ for $j=0,1,2$. Since $\sum_i\tilde u_i=0$, any two functions $f$, $g$ on $Q$ satisfy $\sum_{\{i,l\}}\tilde u_i\tilde u_l(f_i-f_l)(g_i-g_l)=-\big(\sum_i\tilde u_if_i\big)\big(\sum_i\tilde u_ig_i\big)$. For $j=1$ we take $f=g=w$. The result vanishes because $\sum_i\tilde u_iw_i=0$. For $j=2$ we write $(w_i-w_l)(z_i+z_l)=\big((wz)_i-(wz)_l\big)+(w_iz_l-w_lz_i)$. The first part gives $-\big(\sum\tilde u_iw_i\big)\big(\sum\tilde u_iw_iz_i\big)=0$. In the second part the pairs through $k$ contribute nothing. On the outer pairs $w_bz_c-w_cz_b=-u_a$ and cyclically, so that the second part equals $-\tilde u_a\tilde u_b\tilde u_c\big((w_b-w_c)+(w_c-w_a)+(w_a-w_b)\big)=0$. The last statement follows from \eqref{eq:G2mass} and $\hat z_k=0$.

label: thm:wtriangle
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:wtriangle}
Let $m_a,m_b,m_c>0$, and let $z_a,z_b,z_c$ be distinct nonzero complex numbers with $\sum_im_iz_i=\sum_im_iz_i^2=0$ and $\sum_im_ix_i=0$ for some $x_i$ with $x_i^2z_i=1$. Then $m_a=m_b=m_c$ and $\{z_a,z_b,z_c\}=\lambda\{1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2\}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The plane $m^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb{C}^3:\sum_im_iv_i=0\}$ contains $z$ and $z^2=(z_i^2)$, which are independent because the $z_i$ are distinct and nonzero. It is closed under complex conjugation because the $m_i$ are real. Hence $\bar z=\alpha z+\beta z^2$. If $\beta=0$, then $|\alpha|=1$ and the $z_i$ lie on a line through $0$, so that $\sum m_iz_i^2\ne0$. Thus $\beta\ne0$. The scaling $z\mapsto\lambda z$, $x\mapsto\lambda^{-1/2}x$ preserves the hypotheses and multiplies $\beta$ by $\bar\lambda/\lambda^2$. So we may take $\beta=1$: $\bar z_i=\alpha z_i+z_i^2$. Conjugating and substituting gives $z_i=|\alpha|^2z_i+(\alpha^2+\bar\alpha)z_i^2+2\alpha z_i^3+z_i^4$. Hence the $z_i$ are the three roots of
\[
g_\alpha(t)=t^3+2\alpha t^2+(\alpha^2+\bar\alpha)t+|\alpha|^2-1.
\]
Thus $z_a+z_b+z_c=-2\alpha$ and $z_az_bz_c=1-|\alpha|^2$. For $i\ne l$ this gives $z_i\bar z_l+\bar z_iz_l=z_iz_l(2\alpha+z_i+z_l)=-z_az_bz_c=|\alpha|^2-1$. Therefore
\[
0=\Big|\sum_im_iz_i\Big|^2=\sum_im_i^2|z_i|^2-(1-|\alpha|^2)\sum_{i<l}m_im_l,
\]
so that $|\alpha|<1$.

Next, $x\in m^\perp$ and hence $x=\gamma z+\delta z^2$. Then $x_i^2z_i=1$ says that $g_\alpha$ divides $t^3(\gamma+\delta t)^2-1$. The remainder modulo $g_\alpha$ has the coefficients
\begin{align*}
q_2&=-2\alpha\gamma^2+2(3\alpha^2-\bar\alpha)\gamma\delta+(1+3\alpha\bar\alpha-4\alpha^3)\delta^2,\\
q_1&=-(\alpha^2+\bar\alpha)\gamma^2+2(2\alpha^3+\alpha\bar\alpha+1)\gamma\delta+(\bar\alpha^2-2\alpha-3\alpha^4)\delta^2
\end{align*}
at $t^2$ and $t$, and a constant coefficient containing $-1$. So $(\gamma,\delta)\ne(0,0)$ is a common zero of the binary quadratic forms $q_2$ and $q_1$. Hence their resultant vanishes: $N(\alpha,\bar\alpha)=0$, where
\[
N(a,b)=4a^7-a^6b^2+6a^5b+2a^4b^3+11a^4+8a^3b^2-a^2b^4+6a^2b+14ab^3+8a+4b^5+3b^2 .
\]
Suppose that $\alpha=\rho e^{i\varphi}\ne0$, so that $0<\rho<1$. Since each monomial $a^ib^j$ of $N$ has $i-j\equiv1\pmod3$, $N(\alpha,\bar\alpha)=\alpha E$ with
\[
E=4\rho^6e^{6i\varphi}+\rho^3(11+6\rho^2-\rho^4)e^{3i\varphi}+2(\rho^6+4\rho^4+3\rho^2+4)+\rho(3+14\rho^2-\rho^4)e^{-3i\varphi}+4\rho^4e^{-6i\varphi}.
\]
Its imaginary part is $\operatorname{Im}E=\rho(\rho^2-1)\sin3\varphi\,(8\rho^3\cos3\varphi-\rho^4+6\rho^2+3)$. The last factor is at least $(1-\rho)(\rho^3+9\rho^2+3\rho+3)>0$. Thus $\sin3\varphi=0$. For $e^{3i\varphi}=1$, $E=-\rho^7+6\rho^6+5\rho^5+12\rho^4+25\rho^3+6\rho^2+3\rho+8>0$. For $e^{3i\varphi}=-1$, $E=(1-\rho)^2(\rho^5+8\rho^4+10\rho^3+24\rho^2+13\rho+8)>0$. This contradicts $E=0$. Therefore $\alpha=0$. Then $g_0(t)=t^3-1$, the $z_i$ are the cube roots of unity, and $\sum m_iz_i=0$ with real $m_i$ forces $m_a=m_b=m_c$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d14blead}

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:Kgating}(a). For $i\in Q$ let $C^z_i=\sum_{l\in Q\setminus i}m_lz_{il}p_{il}^3$ and $C^w_i$ likewise. The identity $p_{il}^3z_{il}w_{il}=p_{il}$ gives
\[
\sum_{i\in Q}m_iw_{ik}C^z_i=\sum_{\{i,l\}\subseteq Q}m_im_lp_{il}=\sum_{i\in Q}m_iz_{ik}C^w_i .
\]
By \eqref{eq:AK4}, $C^z_i=z_i-m_jp_{ij}^3z_{ij}$, whose terms have exponent at least $1$. The left side therefore has exponent at least $2$. Similarly $C^w_i=w_i-m_jp_{ij}^3w_{ij}$. Here $w_i=w_k+v_i$ has the leading term $-\frac{m_j}M\hat w_j$ at exponent $-\sigma$, the term $p_{ij}^3w_{ij}$ has exponent $\frac{\sigma-3}2>-\sigma$ for $i\ne k$, and $p_{kj}^3w_{kj}$ has exponent $-\sigma$ with coefficient $-\hat p_{kj}^3\hat w_j$. Thus $C^w_i$ has the coefficient $m_j\hat w_j\big(-\frac1M+[i=k]\hat p_{kj}^3\big)$ at exponent $-\sigma$. Since $\sum_im_iC^w_i=0$, we obtain $\hat p_{kj}^3=M_Q/(m_kM)$. On the right side the term $i=k$ vanishes. The rest has the coefficient $-\frac{m_j}M\hat w_j\sum_{i\in Q'}m_i\hat z_i$ at exponent $1-\sigma<2$, which therefore vanishes.

label: lem:d14energy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:identities}, $\nabla_yF(\tau,y(\tau))=0$ and $F(\tau,y(\tau))$ is constant. Let $Z=\sum_{i\in Q'}y_{u_i}\partial/\partial y_{u_i}$ and $W=\sum_{i\in Q'}y_{v_i}\partial/\partial y_{v_i}$. The function $U_Q$ is homogeneous of degree $-\frac12$ in the $y_{u_i}$ and in the $y_{v_i}$, $\psi$ is linear in the $y_{u_i}$, and $S_{2n+1}$ is homogeneous of degree $-n-\frac12$ in them. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d14exp}, along $y(\tau)$,
\begin{align*}
0=W\cdot\nabla_yF&=-\tfrac12\tau^{-2}U_Q+O(\tau^4),\\
0=Z\cdot\nabla_yF&=-\tfrac12\tau^{-2}U_Q+\tau^{2-2\sigma}\Gamma-\textstyle\sum_n\big(n+\frac12\big)\tau^{(2n+1)(\sigma-1)}B_n+O(\tau^4).
\end{align*}
The first identity gives (a). The $y_{u_j}$-component of $\nabla_yF=0$ reads $y_{v_j}f'(\Pi)+O(\tau^{3\sigma-3})=0$. As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:order3}, $f'(\bar\Pi)=0\ne f''(\bar\Pi)$, so that $\Pi(\tau)-\bar\Pi=O(\tau^{3\sigma-3})$ and $[f(\Pi(\tau))]_q=0$ for $0<q<6\sigma-6$. Let $\sigma-1\le q\le3\sigma-3$. Then $f$, $R$ and the $B_n$ with $n\ge2$ contribute nothing at $\tau^q$. By (a) neither does $U_Q$. So the coefficients of $\tau^q$ in the second identity and in $F(\tau,y(\tau))$ are
\[
[\Gamma]_{q+2\sigma-2}-\tfrac12[B_0]_{q-\sigma+1}-\tfrac32[B_1]_{q-3\sigma+3}=0,\qquad[\Gamma]_{q+2\sigma-2}+[B_0]_{q-\sigma+1}+[B_1]_{q-3\sigma+3}=0,
\]
and their difference gives $3[B_0]_{q-\sigma+1}+5[B_1]_{q-3\sigma+3}=0$. For $q<3\sigma-3$ the second term vanishes, which is (b). For $q=3\sigma-3$ it is $5B_1(\bar y)$, which is (c). Finally $B_0(\bar y)=m_j(-\hat w_j)^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in Q'}m_ix_i$. The condition $\mathrm{X3}_k$ holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:d14blead}.

label: lem:typeIII
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:typeIII}
Let $m\in(\mathbb{C}^*)^4$ have real ratios $m_i/m_l$. Then no non-collinear configuration of $\mathrm{K14}(m)$ has a pattern of type III.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that one has. We diagonalize the matrix of the pattern and show that $\kappa\ne0$ forces the configuration to be collinear and that $\kappa=0$ is impossible for real mass ratios. After a gauge change, $\eta$ is the pattern above or its complex conjugate. We treat the first. For the second, replace $\mathrm{j}$ by $\mathrm{j}^2$ throughout. Let $H=(\eta_{il})$, with zero diagonal, $u=(m_lt_l)_l$, $e_0=(1,1,1,1)$, $e_1=(1,1,-1,-1)$, $e_2=(1,-1,1,-1)$ and $e_3=(1,-1,-1,1)$. Then \eqref{eq:tsys} reads $Hu=\kappa(t_l^2)_l$ and $\sum_lu_lt_l^2=0$. We have $He_0=0$, $He_1=2e_1$, $He_2=2\mathrm{j}^2e_2$, $He_3=2\mathrm{j} e_3$. Hence the kernel of $H$ is $\mathbb{C} e_0$ and its image, spanned by $e_1,e_2,e_3$, consists of the vectors with coordinate sum $0$.

Suppose first that $\kappa\ne0$. Then $\sum_lt_l^2=0$. We write $(t_l^2)_l=\xi_1e_1+\xi_2e_2+\xi_3e_3$. We obtain $u=\frac\kappa2(\xi_1e_1+\mathrm{j}\xi_2e_2+\mathrm{j}^2\xi_3e_3)+\gamma e_0$ for some $\gamma\in\mathbb{C}$. Since $e_k\cdot e_{k'}=4\delta_{kk'}$, the last equation of \eqref{eq:tsys} becomes $2\kappa(\xi_1^2+\mathrm{j}\xi_2^2+\mathrm{j}^2\xi_3^2)=0$, so that $\xi_1^2+\mathrm{j}\xi_2^2+\mathrm{j}^2\xi_3^2=0$. For three bodies $a,b,c$ put
\[
h_{abc}=(\eta_{ab}t_c^2+\eta_{ac}t_b^2-\eta_{bc}t_a^2)^2-4\eta_{ab}\eta_{ac}t_b^2t_c^2 ,
\]
which is symmetric in $a,b,c$. For $(a,b,c)=(1,2,3)$ we have $\eta_{12}t_3^2+\eta_{13}t_2^2-\eta_{23}t_1^2=2\mathrm{j}^2\xi_1+2\xi_2$ and $4\eta_{12}\eta_{13}t_2^2t_3^2=4\mathrm{j}^2\big(\xi_3^2-(\xi_1-\xi_2)^2\big)$. Expanding gives
\[
h_{123}=-4\big(\xi_1^2+\mathrm{j}\xi_2^2+\mathrm{j}^2\xi_3^2\big)=0 .
\]
The double transpositions of the bodies fix $\eta$, change each $\xi_k$ at most in sign and permute the four sets $\{a,b,c\}$ transitively. Hence $h_{abc}=0$ for any three bodies $a,b,c$. On the other hand $d_{il}=z_{il}w_{il}=p_{il}^{-2}=\lambda_0^{-2/3}\eta_{il}t_i^{-2}t_l^{-2}$ (since $\eta_{il}^{-2}=\eta_{il}$) and $d_{ab}+d_{ac}-d_{bc}=z_{ab}w_{ac}+z_{ac}w_{ab}$, so that
\[
h_{abc}=\lambda_0^{4/3}(t_at_bt_c)^4\big((d_{ab}+d_{ac}-d_{bc})^2-4d_{ab}d_{ac}\big)=\lambda_0^{4/3}(t_at_bt_c)^4(z_{ab}w_{ac}-z_{ac}w_{ab})^2 .
\]
For a real configuration, $w=\bar z$, the factor $(z_{ab}w_{ac}-z_{ac}w_{ab})^2$ is $-16$ times the squared area of the triangle $abc$. For such a configuration this identity is Heron's formula. Since $h_{abc}=0$, $\lambda_0\ne0$ and $t\in(\mathbb{C}^*)^4$, we obtain $z_{ab}w_{ac}=z_{ac}w_{ab}$ for any three bodies $a,b,c$. With $a=1$ and $b=2$ this gives $w_{1c}=\beta z_{1c}$ for all $c$, where $\beta=w_{12}/z_{12}$, that is, $w=\alpha+\beta z$ with $\alpha=w_1-\beta z_1$. The configuration is collinear, a contradiction.

Hence $\kappa=0$. Then $u\in\ker H$, so that $t_l=\gamma/m_l$ with $\gamma\ne0$. The last equation of \eqref{eq:tsys} becomes $\gamma^3\sum_lm_l^{-2}=0$. But $\sum_lm_l^{-2}=m_1^{-2}\sum_l(m_1/m_l)^2$, where the last sum is a sum of squares of nonzero real numbers and hence positive, a contradiction.

label: thm:W
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:W}
Let $m_0,m_1,m_2>0$, $\delta\in\mathbb{C}$, and let $x_0,x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{C}^*$ satisfy $x_i^2=\delta+\mathrm{j}^i$, $\sum_im_ix_i=0$ and $\sum_im_ix_i^{-2}=0$. Then $\delta=0$ and $m_0=m_1=m_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that the hypotheses force $\delta=0$ or the vanishing of an explicit polynomial in $\delta$ and $\bar\delta$, and exclude the second case with $\delta\ne0$ by writing $\delta$ in polar form and using the positivity of the masses. We may assume $\sum_im_i=1$. We put $\nu=\sum_im_i\mathrm{j}^i$ and $\rho=|\delta|$. We use the basis $\mathbb{1}=(1,1,1)$, $\Omega=(\mathrm{j}^i)_i$, $\bar\Omega=(\mathrm{j}^{2i})_i$ of $\mathbb{C}^3$. Since $x_i\ne0$, $\delta\ne-\mathrm{j}^i$, that is, $\delta^3\ne-1$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item From $(\delta+\mathrm{j}^i)(\delta^2-\delta\mathrm{j}^i+\mathrm{j}^{2i})=\delta^3+1$ we obtain $z:=(x_i^{-2})_i=(\delta^2\mathbb{1}-\delta\Omega+\bar\Omega)/(\delta^3+1)$. So $\sum m_ix_i^{-2}=0$ reads $\delta^2-\nu\delta+\bar\nu=0$. With its conjugate this gives $\nu(1-\rho^2)=-(\delta\rho^2+\bar\delta^2)$. If $\rho=1$, then $\delta=-\bar\delta^2$ and $\delta^3=-\delta^2\bar\delta^2=-1$, which is excluded. Hence $\rho\ne1$.
\item The plane $V=\{v:\sum_im_iv_i=0\}$ contains $z$, $\bar z$ and $x$. As the $m_i$ are real, $\bar V=V$. In the basis $(\mathbb{1},\Omega,\bar\Omega)$ the coordinates of $z$ and $\bar z$ are proportional to $(\delta^2,-\delta,1)$ and $(\bar\delta^2,1,-\bar\delta)$, whose cross product $n=(\rho^2-1,\bar\delta^2+\delta^2\bar\delta,\delta^2+\delta\bar\delta^2)$ has $n_0\ne0$. So $z$ and $\bar z$ span $V$ and the coordinates $(\hat x_0,\hat x_1,\hat x_2)$ of $x$ satisfy $n_0\hat x_0+n_1\hat x_1+n_2\hat x_2=0$.
\item Since $\Omega\Omega=\bar\Omega$, $\bar\Omega\bar\Omega=\Omega$ and $\Omega\bar\Omega=\mathbb{1}$ componentwise, $x_i^2=\delta+\mathrm{j}^i$ reads $\hat x_0^2+2\hat x_1\hat x_2=\delta$, $2\hat x_0\hat x_1+\hat x_2^2=1$ and $2\hat x_0\hat x_2+\hat x_1^2=0$. We eliminate $\hat x_0$ by (2). Then $n_0$ times the third equation and $n_0^2$ times the difference of $\delta$ times the second and the first are two binary quadratic forms in $(\hat x_1,\hat x_2)$ with a common zero $(\hat x_1,\hat x_2)\ne(0,0)$, as $x\ne0$. Their resultant, $-3\delta(\rho^2-1)^2N(\delta,\bar\delta)$ $(\dagger)$, therefore vanishes, where $N\in\mathbb{Z}[\delta,\bar\delta]$ has $23$ terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
N={}&4\delta^8\bar\delta^4+4\delta^8\bar\delta+24\delta^7\bar\delta^3-3\delta^7+40\delta^6\bar\delta^5-14\delta^6\bar\delta^2+4\delta^5\bar\delta^7+19\delta^5\bar\delta^4\\
&-12\delta^5\bar\delta+54\delta^4\bar\delta^6-48\delta^4\bar\delta^3+6\delta^4+\delta^3\bar\delta^8-20\delta^3\bar\delta^5+6\delta^3\bar\delta^2+28\delta^2\bar\delta^7\\
&-18\delta^2\bar\delta^4+8\delta^2\bar\delta-12\delta\bar\delta^6+12\delta\bar\delta^3-3\delta+4\bar\delta^8-4\bar\delta^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence $\delta=0$ or $N(\delta,\bar\delta)=0$.
\item Suppose that $\delta=\rho e^{i\varphi}\ne0$ and $N(\delta,\bar\delta)=0$. Since each monomial $\delta^a\bar\delta^b$ of $N$ has $a-b\equiv1\pmod3$, $N=e^{i\varphi}E$ with $E$ a polynomial in $\rho$ and $e^{\pm3i\varphi}$ with real coefficients. With $c=\cos3\varphi$, $\operatorname{Re}E$ is a polynomial in $\rho$ and $c$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Re}E={}&16\rho^8c^3+(2\rho^{11}+64\rho^9-30\rho^7)c^2+(8\rho^{12}+78\rho^{10}-46\rho^8-30\rho^6+18\rho^4-4\rho^2)c\\
&+39\rho^{11}-13\rho^9-33\rho^7+6\rho^5+8\rho^3-3\rho,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Im}E=-2\rho^2\sin3\varphi\,K,\qquad K=8\rho^6c^2+(\rho^9+24\rho^7-9\rho^5)c+15\rho^8-5\rho^6-3\rho^4+3\rho^2-2\quad(\dagger),
\]
\[
\operatorname{Res}_c(\operatorname{Re}E,K)=7776\rho^{24}(\rho-1)^6(\rho+1)^6(4\rho^8+13\rho^6+27\rho^4+26\rho^2+11)\quad(\dagger).
\]
The resultant is nonzero and $K$ has the leading coefficient $8\rho^6\ne0$. Hence $\operatorname{Re}E$ and $K$ have no common zero, and $\sin3\varphi=0$. If $e^{3i\varphi}=-1$, then $\operatorname{Re}E=-\rho(\rho-1)^4S_-(\rho)$ $(\dagger)$ with $S_-=\rho^4((\rho-1)^2(8\rho+7)+4)+6\rho^3+6\rho^2+8\rho+3>0$. If $e^{3i\varphi}=1$, then $\delta=\rho\mathrm{j}^l$ for some $l$, and replacing $x_i$ and $m_i$ by $\mathrm{j}^lx_{i+l}$ and $m_{i+l}$ we may take $\delta=\rho$. By (1), $\nu=-\rho^2/(1-\rho)$ is real. Thus $m_1=m_2$, $3m_0=1+2\nu$ and $3m_1=1-\nu$. For $\rho>1$ this gives $3m_1(\rho-1)=-(\rho^2-\rho+1)<0$, which contradicts $m_1>0$. For $\rho<1$ it gives $3m_0(1-\rho)=(1-2\rho)(1+\rho)$, so that $\rho<\frac12$. Then $\operatorname{Re}E=\rho(\rho+1)^4S_+(\rho)$ $(\dagger)$ with $S_+=(-3+8\rho-6\rho^2)+\rho^3(6-11\rho)+\rho^5(-6+9\rho+8\rho^2)\le-\frac12+\frac{2187}{21296}+\frac1{64}<0$: on $[0,\frac12]$ the first summand is increasing, the second is at most its value $\frac{2187}{21296}$ at $\rho=\frac9{22}$, and $-6+9\rho+8\rho^2\le\frac12$. In the remaining cases $E\ne0$, a contradiction.
\item Hence $\delta=0$. Then $\bar\nu=0$ by (1), and $m_0=m_1=m_2$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:classI}
Let $m_a,m_b,m_c>0$ and $m_k\ne0$, and let $(z,w,p)$ be a non-collinear $\mathrm{K14}(m_Q)$ configuration of type I with $z_k=w_k=0$ that satisfies $\mathrm{X3}_k$ and has a bad shape. Then $m_a=m_b=m_c$, $(m_k/m_a)^2=\frac13$, and after a relabelling of $a,b,c$, $z=s(1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2)$ and $w=s'(1,\mathrm{j}^2,\mathrm{j})$ with $s,s'\in\mathbb{C}^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion}(a), $(z'_i-z'_l)(w'_i-w'_l)=\Lambda\ne0$ for the three pairs of $Q'$. Let $A=w'_a-w'_b$, $B=w'_b-w'_c$ and $C=w'_c-w'_a$. The corresponding differences of the $z'_i$ are $\Lambda/A$, $\Lambda/B$ and $\Lambda/C$. As their sum is $0$, $AB+BC+CA=0$. With $A+B+C=0$, the numbers $A$, $B$, $C$ are the three roots of $X^3=ABC$. So $w'$ is an equilateral triangle and $z'$ is one of the opposite orientation. Scaling $z$ and $w$, which preserves $\mathrm{K14}$, $\mathrm{X3}_k$ and the bad shape, and labelling the outer bodies $0,1,2$, we obtain $w'_i=\delta+\mathrm{j}^i$ and $z'_i=\gamma+\mathrm{j}^{-i}$ with $\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb{C}$. Then $x_i^2=1/z_i=\delta+\mathrm{j}^i$. The condition $\mathrm{X3}_k$ is $\sum m_ix_i^{-2}=0$. Theorem~\ref{thm:W} gives $\delta=0$ and $m_0=m_1=m_2$. Now $u'_i=(\mathrm{j}^2-\mathrm{j})(\gamma\mathrm{j}^i-1)$ and $p_{ik}^2=z'_iw'_i=\gamma\mathrm{j}^i+1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion}(b), the three numbers $(\gamma\mathrm{j}^i-1)^2/(\gamma\mathrm{j}^i+1)$ equal one number $\varkappa$. If $\gamma\ne0$, the three distinct numbers $\gamma\mathrm{j}^i$ are roots of the quadratic $(X-1)^2-\varkappa(X+1)$, which is impossible. Hence $\gamma=0$, $z=(1,\mathrm{j}^2,\mathrm{j})$ and $w=(1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2)$. The exchange of $b$ and $c$ gives the stated form. Finally, $m_am_bp_{ab}^3=\lambda_0 v_av_b$ and $m_bm_kp_{bk}^3=\lambda_0 v_bv_k$ give $(m_k/m_a)^2=(v_k/v_a)^2(d_{bk}/d_{ab})^3$. Here $v_a=v_b=v_c=-v_k/3$ by the cross product in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion}, $d_{bk}=1$ and $d_{ab}=3$, so that $(m_k/m_a)^2=\frac13$.

title: Theorem
body_md:

label: eq:heron
title: Proof
body_md:
We parametrize the inverted configuration by three unknowns, derive two polynomial equations in them from the bad shape and $\mathrm{X3}_k$, solve the resulting system exactly over $\mathbb{Q}$, and show in ball arithmetic that at each of its solutions one of the two squared ratios of the outer masses is not positive. We label the outer bodies $0,1,2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion}(a), $(z'_i-z'_l)(w'_i-w'_l)=\theta_{il}\Lambda$, where $\Lambda\ne0$ and $\theta_{01},\theta_{12},\theta_{20}$ are cube roots of unity, exactly two of them equal. After a relabelling, which preserves $\mathrm{K14}$, $\mathrm{X3}_k$ and the bad shape, and a change of $\Lambda$, $(\theta_{01},\theta_{12},\theta_{20})=(1,1,\varpi)$ with $\varpi\in\{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2\}$. Let $A=w'_0-w'_1$ and $B=w'_1-w'_2$. Then $z'_0-z'_1=\Lambda/A$, $z'_1-z'_2=\Lambda/B$ and $z'_2-z'_0=-\varpi\Lambda/(A+B)$. As their sum is $0$, $A^2+(2-\varpi)AB+B^2=0$ $(\dagger)$. So $t=A/B$ satisfies $t^2+(2-\varpi)t+1=0$, that is, $\varpi=(t+1)^2/t$. The condition $\varpi^2+\varpi+1=0$ becomes
\[
f(t)=t^4+5t^3+9t^2+5t+1=0\quad(\dagger).
\]
Scaling $z$ and $w$ we take $B=\Lambda=1$. Then $w'=(\delta,\delta-t,\delta-t-1)$ and $z'=(\gamma,\gamma-1/t,\gamma-1/t-1)$ with $\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb{C}$. The $u'_i$ are affine in $(\gamma,\delta)$ $(\dagger)$. With $\xi_i=p_{ik}/x_i$ we have $\xi_i^2=z'_i$, as $x_i^2=w'_i$. Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion}(b) gives $m_i=C\,u'_i/(x_i\xi_i)$. So the bad shape and $\mathrm{X3}_k$ read
\[
\textstyle\sum_iu'_i/\xi_i=0,\qquad\sum_iu'_i/(x_i^3\xi_i)=0.
\]
For $r\in\mathbb{C}^3$, some choice of signs gives $r_0\pm r_1\pm r_2=0$ if and only if $H(r_0^2,r_1^2,r_2^2)=0$, where $H(h)=\sum_ih_i^2-2\sum_{i<l}h_ih_l$, because $H(r_0^2,r_1^2,r_2^2)$ is the product of the four sums $r_0\pm r_1\pm r_2$ $(\dagger)$. Hence $H(h)=H(h')=0$ for $h_i=u_i'^2/z'_i$ and $h'_i=u_i'^2/(w_i'^3z'_i)$. Clearing denominators, we obtain the polynomials $H_1=t^8(z'_0z'_1z'_2)^2H(h)$ and $H_2=t^8(w_0'^3w_1'^3w_2'^3z'_0z'_1z'_2)^2H(h')$ in $\mathbb{Q}[t,\gamma,\delta]$ $(\dagger)$. Let $S=t\prod_iw'_i\prod_i(tz'_i)\prod_i(tu'_i)$. It does not vanish at a configuration: $t\ne0$ as $f(0)\ne0$, the $z'_i$ and $w'_i$ are finite and nonzero, and $u'_i\ne0$ as $m_i\ne0$. If the outer masses have real ratios, then
\[
R_i=(m_i/m_0)^2=\frac{u_i'^2w'_0z'_0}{u_0'^2w'_iz'_i}\in(0,\infty)\qquad(i=1,2).
\]
It therefore suffices to show that no solution $(t,\gamma,\delta,s)$ of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:heron}
f(t)=H_1=H_2=sS-1=0
\end{equation}
has $R_1,R_2\in(0,\infty)$.

We solve \eqref{eq:heron} exactly over $\mathbb{Q}$. A rational parametrization by the coordinate $\delta$, with a squarefree eliminant of degree $280$ and a denominator that is invertible modulo the eliminant, satisfies the four equations exactly modulo the eliminant. So \eqref{eq:heron} has at least $280$ solutions, with distinct values of $\delta$. To show that it has no others we use a second system $E$, in the unknowns $t,\gamma,\delta$ and $e_i=x_{i+1}x_{i+2}$, $f_i=t\xi_{i+1}\xi_{i+2}$ (indices modulo $3$). It consists of $f(t)$, the relations $e_i^2=w'_{i+1}w'_{i+2}$, $e_ie_l=w'_ne_n$, $f_i^2=(tz'_{i+1})(tz'_{i+2})$ and $f_if_l=(tz'_n)f_n$ for $\{i,l,n\}=\{0,1,2\}$, and the two conditions in the form $\sum_i(tu'_i)f_i=0$ and $\sum_i(tu'_i)e_i^3f_i=0$. Each solution of \eqref{eq:heron} gives a point of $V(E)$ with the same $(t,\gamma,\delta)$, at which $S\ne0$: we choose the signs of the $\xi_i$ so that the first sum vanishes, and then those of the $x_i$ for the second. A standard basis of $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ shows that $E$ has dimension $0$ and that the quotient ring of the polynomial ring by $E$ has dimension $472$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Multiplication by $S$ on this quotient ring has rank $280$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, the quotient ring is the product of the local rings at the points of $V(E)$. On the local ring at a point where $S\ne0$ multiplication by $S$ is invertible. So the rank is at least the total multiplicity of the points of $V(E)$ at which $S\ne0$, there are at most $280$ such points, and the $280$ solutions are all. In ball arithmetic at $800$ bits, with disjoint balls around the roots of the eliminant, at each solution $|\operatorname{Im}R_i|\ge0.0469$ or $\operatorname{Re}R_i\le-0.0469$ for $i=1$ or $i=2$. The programs and their logs are in the supplementary material.

label: thm:col
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:col}
Let $m_a,m_b,m_c,m_k>0$. No collinear $\mathrm{K14}(m_Q)$ configuration with $z_k=0$ satisfies $\mathrm{X3}_k$ and has a bad shape.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $w=\alpha+\beta z$. Then $\beta\ne0$, as no $w_{il}$ vanishes, $w_{il}=\beta z_{il}$, and $p_{il}=s_{il}\beta^{-1/2}/z_{il}$ with $s_{il}=\pm1$ and $s_{li}=-s_{il}$. So $F^w_i=\beta F^z_i$ and $F^z_i=\beta^{-3/2}\sum_{l\ne i}m_ls_{il}/z_{il}^2$. Thus $\mathrm{K14}$ holds if and only if
\[
\textstyle(C_i)\qquad\sum_{l\ne i}m_ls_{il}/z_{il}^2=0\qquad(i\in Q).
\]
We write $z_i=x_i^{-2}$ for $i\in Q'$, with the $x_i$ of the bad shape, $\chi_i=x_i^3$ and $\epsilon_i=s_{ki}$, and $m$, $x$, $x^{-2}$ for the vectors $(m_i)$, $(x_i)$, $(x_i^{-2})$, $i\in Q'$. Then $\mathrm{X3}_k$ and the bad shape say $m\cdot x^{-2}=m\cdot x=0$. The row $(C_k)$ says $\sum_{i\in Q'}m_i\epsilon_ix_i^4=0$.

Suppose first that $x$ and $x^{-2}$ are dependent. Then $\chi_a=\chi_b=\chi_c$, that is, $x_i=\zeta_ix_a$ with $\zeta_i^3=1$. As $m_i>0$, the relation $\sum m_i\zeta_i=0$ forces $\{\zeta_a,\zeta_b,\zeta_c\}=\{1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2\}$ and $m_a=m_b=m_c=:\mu$. Now $(C_k)$ reads $\mu x_a^4\sum\epsilon_i\zeta_i=0$, which forces $\epsilon_a=\epsilon_b=\epsilon_c$. After a scaling of $z$ and a relabelling of $b$ and $c$, $z=(1,\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}^2)$. As $(1-\mathrm{j})^2=-3\mathrm{j}$ and $(1-\mathrm{j}^2)^2=-3\mathrm{j}^2$, the row $(C_a)$ reads $m_ks_{ak}=\frac\mu3(s_{ab}\mathrm{j}^2+s_{ac}\mathrm{j})$. Since $m_k$ is real, $s_{ab}=s_{ac}$ and $m_k=-s_{ak}s_{ab}\mu/3$. In the same way $(C_b)$ and $(C_c)$ give $s_{ba}=s_{bc}$, $m_k=-s_{bk}s_{bc}\mu/3$, and $s_{cb}=s_{ca}$, $m_k=-s_{ck}s_{ca}\mu/3$. As $s_{ik}=-\epsilon_a$ for all $i\in Q'$, $m_k>0$ forces $s_{ab}=s_{bc}=s_{ca}=\epsilon_a$. Then $s_{ac}=s_{ab}=\epsilon_a$ contradicts $s_{ca}=\epsilon_a$.

Hence $x$ and $x^{-2}$ are independent and $m$ is proportional to their cross product, that is, to $(x_a^2(\chi_b-\chi_c),x_b^2(\chi_c-\chi_a),x_c^2(\chi_a-\chi_b))$. In particular the $\chi_i$ are distinct. Now $(C_k)$ says that the rows $(x_i,x_i^{-2},\epsilon_ix_i^4)$, $i\in Q'$, have determinant $0$, that is, after multiplying the rows by $x_i^2$, $\det(\chi_i,1,\epsilon_i\chi_i^2)_{i\in Q'}=0$. If $\epsilon_a=\epsilon_b=\epsilon_c$, this is $\pm$ the Vandermonde determinant of the $\chi_i$ $(\dagger)$, which is nonzero. Otherwise, after the reversal $s\mapsto-s$, which preserves the rows $(C_i)$, and a relabelling, $\epsilon=(1,1,-1)$. The determinant is then $(\chi_b-\chi_a)(2\chi_c^2-(\chi_a-\chi_c)(\chi_b-\chi_c))$ $(\dagger)$. So $(\chi_a-\chi_c)(\chi_b-\chi_c)=2\chi_c^2$. We divide $x$ by $x_c$, which preserves all conditions and the mass ratios, and put $A=\chi_a-1$ and $B=\chi_b-1$. Then $AB=2$, $A\notin\{0,-1,-2,\pm\sqrt2\}$ since the $\chi_i$ are nonzero and distinct, and
\[
m_a/m_c=2x_a^2/(A^2-2),\qquad m_b/m_c=-x_b^2A^2/(A^2-2).
\]
As both are positive, $(x_bA/x_a)^2<0$, $x_b=i\gamma x_a/A$ with $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, and $x_a^2=\rho(A^2-2)$ with $\rho>0$. Taking cubes, with $\chi_a=1+A$ and $\chi_b=(A+2)/A$, we obtain
\[
\textup{(E1)}\quad\gamma^3=iA^2(A+2)/(A+1),\qquad\textup{(E2)}\quad(A+1)^2/(A^2-2)^3=\rho^3>0.
\]
Let $A=u+iv$ with $u,v$ real. Then (E1) gives $P_1=0$ and (E2) gives $P_2=0$, where
\[
P_1=\operatorname{Re}\big(A^2(A+2)(\bar A+1)\big)=u^4+3u^3+2u^2-uv^2-v^4-2v^2\quad(\dagger),\qquad P_2=\operatorname{Im}\big((A+1)^2(\bar A^2-2)^3\big).
\]
Their resultant is $\operatorname{Res}_v(P_1,P_2)=4096u^8(u+1)^3(u+2)h(u)^2$ $(\dagger)$ with $h=2u^3+4u^2-u-4$. The polynomial $P_1$ has the leading coefficient $-1$ in $v$. So $u\in\{0,-1,-2\}$ or $h(u)=0$. For $u=0,-1,-2$, $P_1=-v^2(v^2+2),-v^2(v^2+1),-v^4$, so $v=0$ and $A$ is excluded. The cubic $h$ has discriminant $-104<0$ and hence a single real root $u_0$, and $h(0.917)<0<h(0.918)$, so that $u_0\in(0.917,0.918)$. At $u=u_0$, $P_1=0$ is a quadratic equation in $v^2$ whose roots have the product $-u_0^2(u_0+1)(u_0+2)<0$. Its positive root is $v_0^2=2-u_0^2$, because $P_1=2h(u)$ on the circle $u^2+v^2=2$ $(\dagger)$. Thus $A$ is $A_0=u_0+iv_0$ or $\bar A_0$. If $A=A_0$, then (E1) and (E2) determine $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\rho>0$, hence $x_a$ up to sign, $x_b=i\gamma x_a/A_0$, the positions $z_i=x_i^{-2}$ and the outer mass ratios. Since $m_k$ has the coefficient $s_{ak}/z_a^2\ne0$ in the row $(C_a)$, this row determines $m_k/m_a$ for each choice of $s_{ab},s_{ac}$. Certified in ball arithmetic, the four values are $\pm(0.0059+0.4768i)$ and $\pm(0.1808+0.6951i)$, none of them real. At $\bar A_0$ they are the conjugates. This contradicts $m_k>0$.

title: Proof
body_md: Theorem~\ref{thm:col} excludes collinear configurations. A non-collinear one has a pattern as in \eqref{eq:tsys}. Lemma~\ref{lem:typeIII} and Theorem~\ref{thm:typeII} exclude the types III and II. For type I, Lemma~\ref{lem:classI} gives the masses and, after a relabelling and a scaling of $z$ and $w$, $z=z_{\mathcal E}$ and $w=w_{\mathcal E}$. We scale the masses to $(\sqrt3,\sqrt3,\sqrt3,1)$. Then $d_{il}=3$ on the pairs of $Q'$ and $d_{ik}=1$, so that $p_{il}=e_{il}/\sqrt3$ and $p_{ik}=f_i$ with $e_{il},f_i\in\{\pm1\}$. The rows of $b$ and $c$, divided by $\mathrm{j}$ and $\mathrm{j}^2$, give the same relations, so that $p=\pm p_{\mathcal E}$. Conversely, $\pm p_{\mathcal E}$ solve the rows $F^z_i=0$ for $i\in Q'$ and therefore also $F^z_k=0$. The rows $F^w=0$ are their complex conjugates.

label: lem:d14slice
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d14slice}
Let the configuration be nondegenerate and satisfy $\mathrm{X3}_k$, and let $a\in Q'$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $H_a$ is invertible, and there is a unique analytic map $\lambda\mapsto Y(\lambda)\in(z,w)+\mathcal S_a$, for small $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, with $Y(0)=(z,w)$ and $\partial_l(U_Q-\lambda\psi)(Y(\lambda))=0$ for the four coordinates $l\ne u_a,v_a$.
\item Let $U_Q(Y(\lambda))=\sum_h\alpha_h\lambda^h$ and $\psi(Y(\lambda))=\sum_h\psi_h\lambda^h$. Then $\alpha_0=\psi_0=0$ and $h\alpha_h=(h-1)\psi_{h-1}$ for $h\ge1$. If $\xi\in\mathcal S_a$ and the components of $H\xi-g$ along $\mathcal S_a$ vanish, then $\psi_1=g\cdot\xi$ and $\psi_2=-\frac12D^3U_Q[\xi,\xi,\xi]$.
\item Replace $(z,w,p)$ by $(sz,s'w,\zeta p)$ with $\zeta^2ss'=1$ and $m$ by $cm$ with $c\ne0$, and relabel the outer bodies together with $a$. The new configuration is nondegenerate, and $\psi_h$ is multiplied by $c^{1-h}s(s/\zeta)^h$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Let $\xi\in\mathcal S_a$ with $H_a\xi=0$. Then $H\xi=\beta e_{u_a}+\beta'e_{v_a}$. Pairing with $Z$ and $W$ gives $\beta z_a=\beta'w_a=0$. So $H\xi=0$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{C} Z+\mathbb{C} W$ with $\xi_{u_a}=\xi_{v_a}=0$. Since $z_a,w_a\ne0$, $\xi=0$. The implicit function theorem gives $Y$.
(b) $\alpha_0=U_Q(z,w)=0$ (\S\ref{ss:Kgating}). By $\mathrm{X3}_k$, $\psi_0=0$. Let $\hat F(\lambda)=(U_Q-\lambda\psi)(Y(\lambda))=\sum_hf_h\lambda^h$. The gradient of $U_Q-\lambda\psi$ at $Y(\lambda)$ has only the components $u_a$ and $v_a$, and $Y'(\lambda)\in\mathcal S_a$. So $\hat F'(\lambda)=-\psi(Y(\lambda))$ and $U_Q(Y(\lambda))=\hat F-\lambda\hat F'$. Hence $\alpha_h=(1-h)f_h$ and $\psi_{h-1}=-hf_h$. Next, $Y(\lambda)=(z,w)+\lambda\xi+\lambda^2\eta+O(\lambda^3)$, where $\eta\in\mathcal S_a$ and the components of $H\eta+\frac12D^3U_Q[\xi,\xi]$ along $\mathcal S_a$ vanish. As $\psi$ is linear and $H$ is symmetric, $\psi_1=g\cdot\xi$ and $\psi_2=g\cdot\eta=\xi\cdot H\eta=-\frac12D^3U_Q[\xi,\xi,\xi]$.
(c) Near the two configurations, $U_Q(sz',s'w')=\zeta\,U_Q(z',w')$ for the branches of the $p_{il}$, and $\psi(sz')=s\psi(z')$. So the equations of (a) for the new configuration at $\lambda$ are those for the old one at $(s/\zeta)\lambda$, after the substitution $(z',w')\mapsto(sz',s'w')$. This multiplies $\psi_h$ by $s(s/\zeta)^h$. Under $m\mapsto cm$, $U_Q$ and $\psi$ are multiplied by $c^2$ and $c$. Thus $Y(\lambda)$ becomes $Y(\lambda/c)$ and $\psi_h$ is multiplied by $c^{1-h}$. The Hessian becomes $\zeta D^{-1}HD^{-1}$ with $D=\mathrm{diag}(s,s,s,s',s',s')$, resp.\ $c^2H$, and a relabelling permutes the coordinates, so that nondegeneracy is preserved.

label: prop:resonant
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:resonant}
Let $\sigma=(2n+1)/(n+1)$ for an integer $n\ge1$. If the leading cluster configuration at a place of type $\sigma_k(j)(t)$, $\sigma=1+t$, is nondegenerate, then $\psi_1=\psi_2=0$ for each $a\in Q'$.

title: Proof
body_md: We normalize the place for $a$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:d14follow}. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:d14energy}(a) and~\ref{lem:d14follow}, $\sum_h\alpha_h\lambda(\tau)^h=U_Q(Y(\lambda(\tau)))=O(\tau^{5-\sigma})$. So $\alpha_h=0$ whenever $h(4-2\sigma)<5-\sigma$. As $\sigma\ge\frac32>\frac75$, this holds for $h=2$ and $h=3$. Then Lemma~\ref{lem:d14slice}(b) gives $\psi_1=2\alpha_2=0$ and $\psi_2=\frac32\alpha_3=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let a singular place $P$ have type $\sigma_k(j)(t)$ with $0<t<1$, and let $\sigma=1+t$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:d14blead} and~\ref{lem:d14energy}(b), the leading cluster configuration is a $\mathrm{K14}(m_Q)$ configuration that satisfies $\mathrm{X3}_k$ and has a bad shape. By Theorem~\ref{thm:Xhat}, $m_Q=c(\sqrt3,\sqrt3,\sqrt3,1)$ with $c>0$, and after a relabelling of $a,b,c$ the leading cluster configuration is $(sz_{\mathcal E},s'w_{\mathcal E},\zeta p_{\mathcal E})$ with $\zeta^2ss'=1$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:Pdata} and~\ref{lem:d14slice}(c) it is nondegenerate. If $\sigma$ is not of the form $(2n+1)/(n+1)$, Proposition~\ref{prop:D14N} gives a contradiction. Otherwise we take the slice of the outer body that corresponds to $a$ in $\mathcal E$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:Pdata} and~\ref{lem:d14slice}(c), $\psi_2=c^{-1}s(s/\zeta)^2\cdot40/\sqrt3\ne0$, which contradicts Proposition~\ref{prop:resonant}.

label: rem:d14a
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:d14a}
The identities of \S\ref{ss:expansion} also apply at a place of type $\mathsf{u}_0(j)$, the piece $\mathsf{d14a}(j)$, where the fifth body stays at distance of order one from the cluster while the cluster shrinks. There the pairings of $\nabla_yV$ with the $z$- and $w$-scalings of the cluster, together with the constancy of $V$, give at first order a signed dipole condition $\sum_ls_lm_l(\hat z_l-\hat z_G)=0$ when the leading coefficients $\hat p_{jl}$ have unequal signs $s_l$, a centred quadrupole condition $\sum_lm_l(\hat z_l-\hat z_G)^2=0$ when they have equal signs, the same conditions in $w$ at the next order, and in the boundary case a single scalar $g^{\mathsf T}H^+g$. These are the first-order conditions of the analysis of $\mathsf{d14a}$ in \S\ref{sec:curves}. The identities of \S\ref{ss:expansion} therefore do not exclude $\mathsf{d14a}$ at every positive mass: unlike the conditions of Theorems~\ref{thm:order3} and \ref{thm:order5}, these conditions hold at some symmetric K14 configurations with positive masses, for instance centrally symmetric ones. We treat the pieces $\mathsf{d14a}$ instead by the point certificates of \S\ref{sec:points}.

Likewise $w_{kl}=\tau^{2\omega_{kl}}(\bar w_{kl}+\tau^2c'_{kl})$. \[

title: Proof
body_md: Since the set $Z$ in question is constructible and defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, it is finite or contains a nonempty Zariski open subset of $X$. title: Proof
body_md:
The flats, their sets $G$, their lists of children and the closures are the outcome of the computation. The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:S} uses the lists of children of $35545$ pairs $(P,\ell)$, many of them empty. On the empty face $22$ of the $55$ labels have a component: the ten labels $\mathsf{E}$, the ten labels $\mathsf{R}(ab;s)$ with $s<a<b$, and $\mathsf{H}(25|34)$ and $\mathsf{H}(15|34)$. On this face $110$ decompositions are redone with saturations, and $60$ flats are saturated ideals. They all have dimension~$1$ and satisfy (b) or (c). The computation decides $2599$ label sets: $1840$ are certified, $703$ have an exact witness in the sense of \S\ref{ss:T458}, and $56$ remain undecided.

The $77$ flats outside (a)--(c) are zero-dimensional and expanded. Of them $73$ belong to the empty face, three to $12|3|4|5$ and one to $1|2|3|45$. We decompose each of them into primes. We add the squarefree parts of its univariate eliminants, which gives its radical (Seidenberg's lemma). We take a linear form whose minimal polynomial on the radical has as many roots as the radical has zeros, and we factor this polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$. This gives $334$ primes. Of them $310$ fail (F2) and $18$ fail (F3). For each of the other six we compute a shape basis for a separating linear form and isolate the real roots of its univariate polynomial exactly (class (C2)). Two of these roots give points of $\Sigma_F$: the point $\mathbf q_*$, a zero of a prime of degree $48$ of the empty face, and the point $\mathbf p_*$ of $1|2|3|45$. The other four primes have no real zero in $\Sigma_F$.

$T_1$ and $T_2$: we scale so that $m_2=m_5=1$ and $m_3=m_4=t^2$ with $t>0$ ($T_1$), resp.\ $m_3=m_4=m_5=1$ and $m_2=t^2$ ($T_2$). Then $\mathsf{R}(23;1)$ gives $m_1=t^3/(1+t^2)^2$. So $(1+t^2)^2m$ is the point $t$ of the family.

Replacing $q$ by $-q$ in the case of the minus sign, $x_2=q^2$, $x_1=(1+q^4)/|q|$ and $x_3=(1+q^3+q^4)/|q|$ with $q\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. Hence $m$ is a multiple of the point $q$ of $T_5$, resp.\ of the point $(r,q)$ of $T_8$.

$\mathrm{RL}$: since $x_2=x_3=x_4$, $\mathsf{E}(123)$ forces $x_1=2x_2$. Hence $m$ is a multiple of $(1,4,4,4,\mu)$; the exchange of $1$ and $2$ maps the point $\mu$ of $\mathrm{RL}$ to this vector.

$T_9$: since $x_2=x_3$, $\mathsf{E}(123)$ forces $x_1=2x_2$. Scale so that $x_4=1$ and put $x_2=u^2$, $u>0$. Then $\mathsf{R}(24;1)$ reads $2u^2=(u^4+1)/u$, that is, $(u-1)(u^3-u^2-u-1)=0$. For $u=1$, $m$ is a multiple of $(1,4,4,4,\mu)$ as for $\mathrm{RL}$. body_md: By Proposition~\ref{prop:raycount} there are $306$, resp.\ $294$, orbits, all nondegenerate. With the $60$ collinear ones, we obtain $183$ and $177$ up to similarity. The shape counts are those of the classification. The reflection pairs the non-collinear orbits with equal shapes and reversed cyclic orders. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:slice}, positive scaling of the masses multiplies the normalized central configurations by $t^{1/3}$, and permutations of the masses relabel them. Since both preserve nondegeneracy, collinearity and shapes, the statements hold on the whole rays and for all relabellings.

title: Remark
body_md: By nondegeneracy and the implicit function theorem, the numbers in Theorems~\ref{thm:count1} and~\ref{thm:count2} persist on open neighbourhoods of the two mass vectors that are invariant under positive scaling.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:P1hand}
The method of \cite{Tom26} also gives finiteness at $P_1$ without the count of Theorem~\ref{thm:countP1}. At every positive multiple $m$ of a permutation of $P_1$, the function $U$ vanishes identically on every irreducible curve in the slice $Y_m$ of \S\ref{ss:slice}. So $m$ is settled, and it has finitely many central configurations up to similarity. This is part of \cite{Tom26}.

label: rem:AB
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:AB}
At $m=(1,4,4,4,4)$ the slice $Y_m$ of \S\ref{ss:slice} is the union of $36$ pairwise disjoint irreducible curves and a finite set. Through the correspondence of Lemma~\ref{lem:slice}(a) between the points of $Y_m$ and the solutions of \eqref{eq:AK4}, the curves contain the modified Roberts continuum of \S\ref{sec:intro}, carried to these masses by the exchange of the bodies $1$ and $5$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:slice}(b)), and no point of the curves corresponds to a positive normalized central configuration. At $m=(1,1,4,4,4)$ the slice $Y_m$ is finite. Both statements are proved in \cite{Tom26}. They give a second proof, by a different method, that every point of the special rays has finitely many central configurations up to similarity, but they do not give the counts.

label: thm:hulls
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:hulls}
Consider the model of $V_2^{\mathrm w}$, $V_2$ or $V_N$ \textup{(}\S\ref{ss:d5}\textup{)} for a pair of modes. The projection to $y$ of each point of the model lies in the polytope that Table~\ref{tab:d5hulls} gives for this hull and this pair of modes, up to the exchanges of Lemma~\ref{lem:d5sym}; where the table gives $\emptyset$, the model is empty. In the centred case, the model of Theorem~C0 of the supplementary material is empty for the pairs of modes \textup{(Z1,\,Zs$_{t_0}$)} and \textup{(W1,\,Ws$_{t_0}$)} and their exchanges, where $t_0$ is the body of $T$ at the centre of mass of $T$.
head: environment

label: lem:d5sym
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d5sym}
The exchange of the colours maps the model of each hull, and that of the centred case, for a pair of modes onto the model of the same kind for the pair with Z1, Zs and W1, Ws exchanged, and it fixes $y$. The exchange of $A$ and $B$ maps the model for a pair of modes $(a,b)$ onto the model for $(b,a)$, and $y$ to $(y_3,y_4,y_1,y_2,y_5)$. Every pair of modes is the image of one of the nine pairs of Table~\ref{tab:d5hulls} under these exchanges.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The system \eqref{eq:AK4} and the type are invariant under the exchange of $z$ and $w$. This exchange maps each relation of a model to a relation of the model for the pair of modes with the colours exchanged: (P), (E) and (F) in $z$ go to their counterparts in $w$, (V) goes to (V$'$), and (S), (Q), (R), (T) go to their mirror images. The exchange of $A$ and $B$ renames the outer bodies. The two exchanges generate a group of order $4$, whose orbits on the $25$ pairs of modes are those of the nine pairs of the table.
head: environment

label: lem:d5rules
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d5rules}
At every point of the model of $V_2^{\mathrm w}$, for $X\in\{A,B\}$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item In each colour, five of the six orders $c_A$, $c_B$, $\zeta$, $p^z_A$, $p^z_B$, $p^z_c$ are equal to their minimum $\mu_z$, and the sixth, the \emph{exception}, is at least $\mu_z$; likewise in $w$, with the minimum $\mu_w$. So if two of the six orders differ, the larger is the exception and the other five are equal to the smaller. If $c_A,c_B\ge1$, then $\zeta\ge1$ and $p^z_A,p^z_B,p^z_c\ge1$.
\item $t^z_X\ge\min(p^z_X,\zeta-3r)$, with equality if $p^z_X\ne\zeta-3r$. If $r<0$ and $p^z_X=\mu_z$, then $t^z_X=\mu_z$. The same holds in $w$.
\item In the modes F and Z1, $d_X+t^z_X\ge-\bar x_X$, with equality in mode F in the models of $V_2$ and $V_N$. In mode Zs, $d_X+t^z_X=-x^0_X$.
\item In mode Z1, $3\bar x_X<2+f_X$; in mode Zs, $3x^0_X<2+f_X$. Moreover $3r<2+\zeta$ and $3r<2+\omega$.
\item In the modes Z1 and Zs, $c_X+d_X\ge1+f_X=2\bar x_X$. If $r>0$, the minimum of $c_A+d_A$, $c_B+d_B$ and $0$ is attained at least twice. If $r<0$, the minimum of $2r$, $c_A+d_A$ and $c_B+d_B$ is attained at least twice, and it is at most $2r$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (a) If two of the six orders exceeded the minimum, they would form, with an order equal to the minimum, a triple whose minimum is attained once, against (P). If $c_A,c_B\ge1$ and $\mu_z<1$, both $c_A$ and $c_B$ would be exceptions. (b) is (E): the two smallest of $p^z_X$, $\zeta-3r$ and $t^z_X$ are equal. If $r<0$, then $\zeta-3r>\zeta\ge\mu_z$. (c) follows from (S); for example, in mode F, $d_X+t^z_X\ge d_X+c_X-3\bar x_X=-\bar x_X$. (d) restates $f_X<1$, $3s_X+f_X<4$, $\zeta+3\omega<4$ and $3\zeta+\omega<4$. (e) The inequality holds as $c_X\ge1$. The rest is (I), whose minimum is at most $0<2r$ if $r>0$, and at most $2r<0$ if $r<0$.

label: prop:d5empty
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:d5empty}
The models of the pairs of modes \textup{(F,\,Zs)}, \textup{(Z1,\,Ws)} and \textup{(Zs,\,Ws)} are empty.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B$ be in mode Ws$_{t_0}$, with the far order $g:=c_B<1$, so that $d_B\ge1$, $s_B>1$, $x^0_B=\frac12(s_B+g)$, $t^z_B=g-3x^0_B$ and $t^w_B=s_B-3x^0_B$. Let $A$ be in mode Z1 or Zs. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $c_B<1\le c_A$ gives $\zeta=p^z_A=p^z_B=p^z_c=g$, and $d_A<1\le d_B$ gives $\omega=p^w_A=p^w_B=p^w_c=f_A$. So $2r=f_A+g$. In $z$, relation (E) for $B$ says that the maximum of $0$, $r$, $x^0_B$ is attained twice. In $w$, since $t^w_B-f_A=-x^0_B-2r$, it says that the maximum of $0$, $3r$, $x^0_B+2r$ is attained twice. If $r>0$, the first statement gives $x^0_B=r$, hence $s_B=f_A<1$. If $r<0$, it gives $x^0_B=0$, and then $0$ is the only maximum in the second. If $r=0$, it gives $x^0_B\le0$, hence $s_B\le-g=f_A<1$. Each case contradicts $s_B>1$.

Now let $A$ be in mode F and $B$ in mode Zs$_{t_0}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $c_A<1\le c_B$ gives $\zeta=c_A=p^z_A=p^z_B=p^z_c=:\kappa<1$. Thus $\omega=2r-\kappa$.

If $r>0$, then $\zeta-3r<\kappa$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_A=t^z_B=\kappa-3r$. By (S), $t^z_A\ge\kappa-3\bar x_A$. Hence $\bar x_A\ge r$, that is, $d_A\ge\omega$. And $t^z_B=-\frac12(s_B+3f_B)=\kappa-3r$ with $s_B>1$ gives $f_B<2r-\frac13(2\kappa+1)<\omega$. So $\omega$ and $d_A$ both exceed $f_B$ and both are exceptions in $w$.

If $r<0$, then $\zeta-3r>\kappa$, and $t^z_A=t^z_B=\kappa$. For $A$ this gives $\bar x_A\ge0$. Thus $d_A\ge-\kappa>\omega$. So $d_A$ is the exception in $w$ and $f_B=\omega=p^w_B$. For $B$ it gives $f_B=-\frac13(2\kappa+s_B)$. As $\omega-3r>p^w_B$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_B=p^w_B=f_B$. Then $x^0_B=0$, $s_B=-f_B$ and $f_B=-\kappa$, whereas $f_B=\omega<-\kappa$.

If $r=0$, then $t^z_B\ge\kappa$, so $s_B+3f_B\le-2\kappa$ and $f_B<-\frac13(2\kappa+1)<-\kappa=\omega$. So $\omega$ is the exception in $w$ and $d_A=f_B=p^w_A<\omega$. Hence $t^w_A=f_B$, while (S) gives $t^w_A\ge d_A-3\bar x_A=-\frac12(3\kappa+f_B)$, that is, $f_B\ge-\kappa$.

label: prop:d5zero
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Let $g=c_B<1$ be the far order of $B$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $\zeta=g$ and $\omega=f_A$. Thus $2r=f_A+g$. Since $c_A+d_A\ge1+f_A>2r$ and $c_B+d_B\ge1+g>2r$, the minimum in (I) is attained by $2r$ and $0$. So $r=0$ and $\bar x_A+\bar x_B=1+\frac12(f_A+g)=1$.

(b) Suppose that $r>0$. Since the minimum in (V) is at most $-r<0$, it is attained by $d_X+t^z_X$ for some $X$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(c) gives $\bar x_X\ge r>0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e), the other body $Y$ has $c_Y+d_Y=0$. The minimum of $c_A$, $c_B$, $\zeta$ is attained twice. So $c_Y\ge\min(c_X,\zeta)$, and likewise $d_Y\ge\min(d_X,\omega)$; hence $0=c_Y+d_Y\ge\min(c_X,\zeta)+\min(d_X,\omega)$. As $c_X+d_X>0$ and $\zeta+\omega>0$, either $c_X\le\zeta$ and $\omega\le d_X$, or $\zeta\le c_X$ and $d_X\le\omega$. In the first case also $\omega\le d_Y$. Thus $\omega=\mu_w$. Then $p^w_Y\ge\omega>\omega-3r$ and $t^w_Y\ge d_Y-3\bar x_Y=d_Y\ge\omega$ by (S). Hence the minimum $\omega-3r$ in (E) is attained once. The second case is the same in $z$.

Suppose that $r<0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e), $c_X+d_X\le2r$ for some $X$. Then $\bar x_X<0$ and $d_X+t^z_X\ge-\bar x_X>0$. As $-r>0$, the minimum in (V) is $0$, attained also by $d_Y+t^z_Y\ge-\bar x_Y$. Hence $\bar x_Y\ge0$. Then $c_Y$ and $d_Y$ are not both minimal in their colours, since otherwise $2\bar x_Y\le c_X+d_X<0$. Say that $c_Y$ is the exception in $z$. Then $p^z_X=c_X=\mu_z$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_X=c_X$, against $t^z_X\ge c_X-3\bar x_X>c_X$. The case of $d_Y$ is the same in $w$.

So $r=0$. If $\bar x_A<0$, then $c_A+d_A<\zeta+\omega$; say $c_A<\zeta$. Then $\zeta$ is the exception in $z$ and $p^z_A=c_A<\zeta-3r$. So $t^z_A=c_A$, against $t^z_A\ge c_A-3\bar x_A>c_A$. Hence $\bar x_A,\bar x_B\ge0$. If $\zeta$ were the exception in $z$, then $c_A=c_B=\mu_z$ and $\omega=-\zeta<-\mu_z\le d_A,d_B$, which would give two exceptions in $w$. So $\zeta=\mu_z$, likewise $\omega=\mu_w$, and $\mu_z+\mu_w=0$. One of $c_A$, $c_B$ is equal to $\mu_z$ and one of $d_A$, $d_B$ to $\mu_w$. Hence $\bar x_A+\bar x_B$ is half the sum of the two other orders among $c_A$, $d_A$, $c_B$, $d_B$, which are less than $1$. In the models of $V_2$ and $V_N$, (S) and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) give $c_A-3\bar x_A=t^z_A\ge\mu_z$ and $d_A-3\bar x_A\ge\mu_w$. Adding, we obtain $-4\bar x_A\ge0$. So $\bar x_A=0$ and likewise $\bar x_B=0$.

(c) By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $c_A<1\le c_B$ gives $\zeta=c_A=p^z_A=p^z_B=p^z_c=:\kappa<1$. If $r>0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_A=t^z_B=\kappa-3r$. For $A$, (S) then gives $\bar x_A\ge r>0$. Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e) gives $c_B+f_B=0$ and $f_B\le-1$. For $B$, (S) gives $\kappa-3r\ge1-3\bar x_B$, that is, $f_B\ge2r-\frac13(2\kappa+1)>-1$. If $r<0$, then $t^z_A=t^z_B=\kappa$, so $\bar x_A\ge0$ and $f_B\ge-\frac13(2\kappa+1)>-1$. Then $c_A+d_A>2r$ and $c_B+f_B>0>2r$, against Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e). So $r=0$ and $\omega=-\kappa$. As in (b), $\bar x_A\ge0$. So $\omega$ is not the exception in $w$, since otherwise $d_A=\mu_w<\omega$ and $\bar x_A<0$. Hence $\omega=\mu_w=-\kappa>-1$. Then $f_B\ge-\kappa$ gives $\bar x_B>0$. One of $d_A$, $f_B$ is equal to $-\kappa$. If $d_A=-\kappa$, then $\bar x_A=0$ and $\bar x_B<1$. If $f_B=-\kappa$, then $\bar x_A+\bar x_B=\frac12(\kappa+d_A)+\frac12(1-\kappa)=\frac12(1+d_A)<1$. In the model of $V_2$, (S) and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) give $\kappa-3\bar x_A=t^z_A\ge\kappa$, so $\bar x_A=0$.

(d) By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $\zeta\ge1$. Suppose that $r>0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e), $c_X+f_X\le0$ for some $X$. Then $f_X\le-1$ and $\bar x_X\le0$. As in (b), (V) gives $d_Y+t^z_Y\le-r$ for some $Y$. Hence $\bar x_Y\ge r>0$. Thus $Y\ne X$ and $f_X<f_Y$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $f_X=\omega=p^w_X=\mu_w$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_X=\omega-3r<f_X$, against $t^w_X\ge f_X-3\bar x_X\ge f_X$. Suppose that $r<0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e), $c_X+f_X\le2r$ for some $X$. Then $f_X<-1$ and $\bar x_X<0$. As in (b), the minimum in (V) is $0=d_Y+t^z_Y$. Hence $\bar x_Y\ge0$ and $f_Y\ge-1>f_X$. Then $p^w_X=f_X=\mu_w$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_X=f_X$, against $t^w_X\ge f_X-3\bar x_X>f_X$. So $r=0$ and $\omega=-\zeta\le-1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), one of $f_A$, $f_B$ is equal to $\mu_w\le\omega$, and the other is less than $1$.
