label: prop:d5ss
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:d5ss}
Let both outer bodies be in mode Zs. At every point of the model of $V_2^{\mathrm w}$, $r\ge0$ and $x^0_A,x^0_B\le r$. If $r>0$, then $y$ lies in the triangle $\mathcal T=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,-\frac12,0,-\frac12,0),\,0,\,(\frac13,0,\frac13,0,\frac13)\}$. If $r=0$, then $y$ lies in the polytope $\mathcal R$ of the points with $y_5=0$, $y_2\le y_1\le0$, $y_4\le y_3\le0$, $y_2,y_4\ge-\frac12$ and
\[
3y_4\le y_1+2y_2\le2y_4,\qquad 3y_2\le y_3+2y_4\le2y_2 .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a body $X$ in mode Zs, $t^z_X=s_X-3x^0_X=1-x^0_X-2\bar x_X$ and $t^w_X=f_X-3x^0_X$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(c), relation (V) says that the maximum of $x^0_A$, $x^0_B$, $r$ and $0$ is attained at least twice. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $\zeta\ge1$ and $p^z_A,p^z_B,p^z_c\ge1$.

\emph{$r\ge0$.} Suppose that $r<0$. If $p^w_A=p^w_B=\mu_w$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_X=\mu_w\le f_X$, so $3x^0_X=f_X-\mu_w\ge0$ for both $X$. If moreover $f_A=f_B=\mu_w$, then $x^0_X=0$ and $t^z_X=s_X=-f_X=-\mu_w$. One of $p^z_A$, $p^z_B$ is equal to $\mu_z$. Hence $t^z_X=\mu_z$ for that $X$, and $2r=\zeta+\omega\ge\mu_z+\mu_w=0$, against $r<0$. If instead $f_A>\mu_w$, then $f_B=\mu_w$ and $x^0_B=0<x^0_A$, so the maximum of $x^0_A$, $x^0_B$, $r$, $0$ is attained once; likewise if $f_B>\mu_w$. If $p^w_A>\mu_w$, then $f_A=f_B=\omega=p^w_B=\mu_w$ and $t^w_B=f_B$, so $x^0_B=0$ and $t^z_B=s_B=-\omega>\zeta\ge\mu_z$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b), $p^z_B\ne\mu_z$, that is, the position of $B$ is the exception in $z$, and $c_A=\zeta=p^z_A=\mu_z$. Then $t^z_A=\zeta$. Thus $x^0_A=-\zeta-f_A=-2r>0$, and the maximum is attained once. The case $p^w_B>\mu_w$ is the same.

\emph{$x^0_X\le r$.} Suppose that $x^0_A>r$. As $r\ge0$, the maximum of $x^0_A$, $x^0_B$, $r$, $0$ exceeds $r$ and $0$. Hence $x^0_A=x^0_B=:q>r$. If $t^w_X<\omega-3r$ for some $X$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $p^w_X=t^w_X=f_X-3q<f_X$, so $f_X$ is the exception in $w$ and $p^w_X=\omega$. Then $\omega<\omega-3r$, against $r\ge0$. So $t^w_X\ge\omega-3r$ for both $X$, that is, $f_X\ge\omega+3(q-r)>\omega$, which gives two exceptions in $w$.

\emph{$r>0$.} Then $x^0_Y=r$ for some $Y$, by the maximum rule. In (E) for $Y$ in $w$, $t^w_Y=f_Y-3r$. We use Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b). If $f_Y>\omega$, then $t^w_Y>\omega-3r$ and $p^w_Y=\omega-3r<\omega$, while $f_Y$ is the exception and $p^w_Y=\omega$. If $f_Y<\omega$, then $p^w_Y=t^w_Y<f_Y$, while $\omega$ is the exception and $p^w_Y=f_Y$. So $f_Y=\omega=\mu_w$. For the other body $X$, $x^0_X<r$ would give $t^w_X>f_X-3r\ge\omega-3r$, hence $p^w_X=\omega-3r<\mu_w$. So $x^0_X=r$ and $f_X=\omega$ as for $Y$. Put $f=\omega$. If $1+f>0$, then $c_A+f>0$ and $c_B+f>0$, and the minimum $0$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e) is attained once. So $f\le-1$, that is, $\bar x_A=\bar x_B=\frac12(1+f)\le0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(d), $3r<2+\omega=1+2\bar x_A$. So $y=(r,\bar x_A,r,\bar x_A,r)$ with $0<3r<1+2\bar x_A$ and $\bar x_A\le0$, which lies in $\mathcal T$.

\emph{$r=0$.} Put $L=\zeta=-\omega$, so that $L\ge1$, $\zeta-3r=L$ and $\omega-3r=-L$. As $x^0_X\le0$, $t^w_X\ge f_X$ and $t^z_X\ge s_X>1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a) and (b), in $z$ either (z1) $\zeta$ is the exception, $c_A=c_B=p^z_A=p^z_B=p^z_c=\mu_z<L$ and $t^z_A=t^z_B=\mu_z$, or (z2) $\zeta=\mu_z=L$ and $t^z_X\ge L$ for both $X$. In $w$ there are four cases:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=3.4em,labelwidth=2.8em,labelsep=0.6em,align=left]
\item[(w1)] $\omega$ is the exception, $f_A=f_B=p^w_A=p^w_B=\mu_w<-L$; then Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_X=f_X$, so $x^0_X=0$ and $t^z_X=s_X=-f_X$;
\item[(w2)] $f_A$ is the exception, and $f_B=\omega=-L<f_A$;
\item[(w3)] the same with $A$ and $B$ exchanged;
\item[(w4)] $f_A=f_B=\omega=-L$.
\end{enumerate}
In the cases (w2)--(w4), (z1) is impossible: for $X$ with $f_X=-L$, $t^z_X=\frac12(3L-s_X)=\mu_z$ would give $x^0_X=\frac12(s_X-L)=L-\mu_z>0$, against $x^0_X\le0$. So $t^z_X\ge L$ for both $X$ in these cases. We show $y\in\mathcal R$. The inequalities $y_2\le y_1\le0$, $y_4\le y_3\le0$ and $y_2,y_4\ge-\frac12$ hold since $s_X>1$, $x^0_X\le0$ and $\bar x_X\ge-\frac12$. As $t^z_X=1-x^0_X-2\bar x_X$ and $f_Y=2\bar x_Y-1$, the other four inequalities say that
\[
-f_Y\le t^z_X\le-\tfrac12(1+3f_Y)\qquad\text{for }\{X,Y\}=\{A,B\}.
\]
The lower bound holds with equality in (w1). In (w2), $t^z_A\ge L=-f_B$ and $t^z_B\ge L>-f_A$; (w3) is the same; and in (w4), $t^z_X\ge L=-f_Y$. For the upper bound, $s_X>1$ gives $t^z_X<-\frac12(1+3f_X)$, which suffices if $f_X\ge f_Y$. It remains to treat (w2) with $X=B$, and (w3) with $X=A$, which is the same. In (F) for $A$ in $w$, the terms are $f_A$, $-L+\beta$ and $t^w_A\ge f_A$. Hence $-L+\beta\ge f_A>-L$, that is, $\beta>0$. In (F) for $B$ in $w$, the terms are $f_B=-L$, $-L+\beta>-L$ and $t^w_B\ge-L$. So $t^w_B=-L=f_B$. Hence $x^0_B=0$, $s_B=L$ and $t^z_B=L$. Finally, $t^z_A\ge L$ gives $3f_A\le-2L-s_A<-2L-1$, that is, $t^z_B=L<-\frac12(1+3f_A)$.

label: prop:d5zs
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Here $y=(\bar x_A,\bar x_A,x^0_B,\bar x_B,r)$, with $\bar x_A=\frac12(1+f_A)<1$, $\bar x_B\ge-\frac12$ and $x^0_B>\bar x_B$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $\zeta\ge1$ and $p^z_A,p^z_B,p^z_c\ge1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(c), (V) says that the minimum of $f_A+t^z_A$, $-x^0_B$, $-r$ and $0$ is attained at least twice, and $f_A+t^z_A\ge-\bar x_A$.

\emph{Step 1: $x^0_B\le\max(r,0)$.} Suppose not. Then the minimum in (V) is attained by $-x^0_B$ and $f_A+t^z_A$. Hence $\bar x_A\ge x^0_B>0$ and $f_A>-1$. If $t^w_B<\omega-3r$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $p^w_B=t^w_B<f_B$, so $f_B$ is the exception in $w$, $p^w_B=\omega=f_A$ and $\omega<\omega-3r$. Then $r<0$ and $\zeta=2r-\omega<1$, against $\zeta\ge1$. Otherwise $f_B\ge\omega+3(x^0_B-r)>\omega$. Thus again $f_B$ is the exception and $f_A=\omega$. If $r\le0$, then $\zeta=2r-\omega<1$ as before. If $r>0$, then $\zeta-3r=-r-\omega>-x^0_B-\omega=t^z_A$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $p^z_A=t^z_A=-x^0_B-\omega$. As $p^z_A\ge1$, we obtain $\omega<-1$, against $\omega=f_A>-1$.

\emph{Step 2: if $r>0$, then $x^0_B=r$.} If $x^0_B<r$, the minimum in (V) is attained by $-r$ and $f_A+t^z_A$, so $\bar x_A\ge r>0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e), $c_B+f_B=0$. Thus $f_B\le-1<f_A$. So $f_A$ is the exception in $w$ and $f_B=\omega=p^w_B$. In (E) for $B$ in $w$, the term $\omega-3r$ is less than $p^w_B=\omega$ and than $t^w_B=\omega-3x^0_B$. Hence the minimum is attained once.

\emph{Step 3: if $r>0$, then $f_B=\omega\le-1$, $t^w_A=\omega-3r$ and $3r\le\bar x_A+2\bar x_B$.} As $x^0_B=r$, (E) for $B$ in $w$ gives $f_B=\omega=\mu_w$, as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:d5ss}. If $c_B+f_B>0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e) gives $c_A+f_A=0$, so $f_B=\mu_w\le f_A\le-1$; otherwise $f_B\le-c_B\le-1$. In (F) for $B$ in $w$, the terms are $\omega$, $\omega+\beta$ and $t^w_B=\omega-3r$. Hence $\beta=-3r$. In (F) for $A$ in $w$, the terms are $f_A\ge\omega>\omega-3r=\omega+\beta$ and $t^w_A$. Thus $t^w_A=\omega-3r$. By (S), $t^w_A\ge f_A-3\bar x_A=-\frac12(3+f_A)$. Hence $6r\le3+f_A+2f_B$, which is $3r\le\bar x_A+2\bar x_B$.

\emph{Step 4: if $r<0$, then $x^0_B=0$, $\bar x_B\le r$ and $\bar x_A+2\bar x_B\ge0$.} Since $x^0_B\le0$ by step 1, $t^w_B\ge f_B$. If $p^w_B=\mu_w$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_B=\mu_w\le f_B\le t^w_B$, so $x^0_B=0$ and $f_B=\mu_w$. If $p^w_B>\mu_w$, then $f_A=f_B=\omega=p^w_A=\mu_w$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_A=f_A$. By (S), $f_A\ge-\frac12(3+f_A)$. Thus $\omega=f_A\ge-1$ and $\zeta=2r-\omega<1$, which is impossible. So $x^0_B=0$ and $f_B=\mu_w$.

Next, $c_B+f_B\le2r$. Otherwise, by Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(e), $c_A+f_A=2r$. Hence $f_A<-1$, $\bar x_A<0$ and $t^w_A\ge f_A-3\bar x_A>f_A$. Then $p^w_A\ne\mu_w$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b). So $f_A=f_B=\omega$. Now $c_B>c_A$ makes $c_B$ the exception in $z$. Hence $p^z_B=\mu_z=\zeta$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_B=\zeta$. As $x^0_B=0$, this gives $s_B=t^z_B=\zeta$ and $x^0_B=\frac12(\zeta+\omega)=r<0$, a contradiction. So $f_B\le2r-c_B\le2r-1$, that is, $\bar x_B\le r$.

Finally, if $p^w_A=\mu_w$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^w_A=\mu_w=f_B$, and (S) gives $f_B\ge-\frac12(3+f_A)$, that is, $\bar x_A+2\bar x_B\ge0$. If $p^w_A>\mu_w$, then $f_A=f_B=\omega$, and $s_B=-f_B$ gives $t^z_B=s_B=-\omega=\zeta-2r$. As $\zeta-2r<\zeta-3r$, (E) for $B$ in $z$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) give $p^z_B=t^z_B>\zeta$. So the position of $B$ is the exception in $z$ and $p^z_A=\zeta=\mu_z$. Then $t^z_A=\zeta$. By (S), $\zeta\ge-\frac12(1+3\omega)$, that is, $\omega\ge-1-4r$. But $\omega=f_B\le2r-1<-1-4r$.

\emph{Step 5: if $r=0$, then $f_B\le f_A$.} Otherwise $f_A=\omega=\mu_w$. In (F) for $B$ in $w$, the terms are $f_B$, $\omega+\beta$ and $t^w_B\ge f_B$. Hence $\beta\ge f_B-\omega>0$. In (F) for $A$ in $w$, the terms are $\omega$, $\omega+\beta>\omega$ and $t^w_A$. Thus $t^w_A=\omega=f_A$, and (S) gives $f_A\ge-1$. Then $\bar x_B>\bar x_A\ge0$. Hence $x^0_B>\bar x_B>0$, against step 1.

Steps 1--5, with $\bar x_A<1$, $\bar x_B\ge-\frac12$ and $x^0_B>\bar x_B$, give the three cases.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since these models contain the relations of the model of $V_2$, Propositions~\ref{prop:d5zero} and~\ref{prop:d5zs} apply to them. By (R), a body $X$ in mode Z1 has at most one event. For each of the other quantities of (R) the opposite inequality holds. With (S), (Q) and (T), this means that $c_X=1$, that $t^z_X$ and $t^w_X$ take their lower bounds $1-3\bar x_X$ and $f_X-3\bar x_X$, that $\tau_X=-\bar x_X$ and, if $Y$ is in mode Zs, that $p^z_A,p^z_B,p^z_c\le1$ and (in the model of $V_N$) that $\tilde t_X=-\bar x_X$, except for the event.

(a) \emph{(Z1,\,W1).} By Proposition~\ref{prop:d5zero}(a) and its proof, $r=0$, $\zeta=g:=c_B$, $\omega=f_A$ and $f_A+g=0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_B\ge g$ and $t^w_B\ge f_A$. If $t^z_B$ took its lower bound $-\frac12(3+g)$, then $g\le-1$. If $t^w_B$ took its lower bound $-\frac12(1+3g)$, then $-\frac12(1+3g)\ge-g$, and again $g\le-1$. As $g=-f_A>-1$, both are events of $B$, against (R).

\emph{(F,\,Z1).} By Proposition~\ref{prop:d5zero}(c) and its proof, $r=0$, $\bar x_A=0$, $\zeta=c_A=:\kappa<1$, $\omega=\mu_w=-\kappa$ and $f_B\ge-\kappa$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_B\ge\kappa$ and $t^w_B\ge-\kappa$. If $t^z_B=-\frac12(1+3f_B)$, then $f_B\le-\frac13(2\kappa+1)<-\kappa$. So $t^z_B$ is the event of $B$. Then $t^w_B=-\frac12(3+f_B)\ge-\kappa$ gives $f_B\le2\kappa-3<-1$, against $f_B\ge-\kappa>-1$.

\emph{(Z1,\,Zs).} Let $A$ be in mode Z1 and $B$ in mode Zs$_{t_0}$, in the model of $V_N$ or in that of the centred case. By Proposition~\ref{prop:d5zs}, $y$ lies in $\mathcal S^0$, $\mathcal S^+$ or $\mathcal S^-$. We say that \emph{det holds} if $p^z_A,p^z_B,p^z_c\le1$; it fails only if this is the event of $A$. As these positions are at least $1$, det means that they are equal to $1=\mu_z$. If det fails, then $c_A=1=\mu_z$.

If $r=0$, then $x^0_B\le0$ and $t^z_B\ge s_B>1$. If det holds, (E) for $B$ in $z$ has the terms $p^z_B=1$, $\zeta\ge1$ and $t^z_B>1$, so $\zeta=1$. If det fails, $\zeta>1$ would make $\zeta$ the exception in $z$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) would give $t^z_B=p^z_B=1$; so again $\zeta=1$ and $\omega=-1$. If $\omega$ were the exception in $w$, then $p^w_A=f_A<-1$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) would give $t^w_A=f_A$, against $t^w_A\ge-\frac12(3+f_A)>f_A$. So $\omega=\mu_w=-1$ and one of $f_A$, $f_B$ is equal to $-1$. As $f_B\le f_A$, this gives $f_B=-1$. Then $\bar x_B=0<x^0_B$, against $x^0_B\le0$.

If $r<0$, then $x^0_B=0$ and $t^z_B=s_B>1$. If det holds, then $p^z_B=1=\mu_z$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_B=1$, against $t^z_B>1$. If det fails, $p^z_B=\mu_z$ would give the same, so the position of $B$ is the exception in $z$ and $c_A=\zeta=p^z_A=1$. Then $t^z_A=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b). As $t^z_A$ takes its lower bound $-\frac12(1+3f_A)$, $f_A=-1$, that is, $\bar x_A=0$. Then $\bar x_A+2\bar x_B\ge0$ gives $\bar x_B\ge0>r$, against $\bar x_B\le r$.

If $r>0$, then $x^0_B=r$ and $f_B=\omega\le-1$, so $s_B=2r-\omega=\zeta>1$ and $t^z_B=\zeta-3r$. In the centred case $c_B>1$. If det holds, $\zeta>1=\mu_z$ makes $\zeta$ the exception in $z$, so $c_B=1$. If det fails, $c_A=1=\mu_z$ makes $c_B$ the exception, so $\zeta=1$. Both are impossible. In the model of $V_N$, suppose first that det holds and that $t^z_A$ and $t^w_A$ take their lower bounds. By (E) for $B$ in $z$, with the terms $p^z_B=1$ and $t^z_B=\zeta-3r$, we have $\zeta-3r\le1$. The equality $t^w_A=\omega-3r=-\frac12(3+f_A)$ gives $f_A=6r-3-2\omega$. If $\zeta-3r<1=p^z_A$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_A=\zeta-3r=-r-\omega$, and $t^z_A=-\frac12(1+3f_A)$ then gives $\omega=2r-1$ and hence $r=\frac12(1+\omega)\le0$. If $\zeta-3r=1$, then $\omega=-1-r$, $f_A=8r-1$, and $t^z_A\ge1$ gives $f_A\le-1$ and hence $r\le0$. Hence the event of $A$ is the failure of det, or $t^z_A$, or $t^w_A$. In each case $\tilde t_A=-\bar x_A$. In (T), $e_1-e_2=\frac12(3-2r-\omega)>0$, as $\omega\le-1$ and $r<1$. Hence $\tilde t_B=e_2=-\frac12(1+\omega)$. If $t^w_A$ takes its lower bound, then $\bar x_A=3r-1-\omega$ and $\tilde t_A=1+\omega-3r<\tilde t_B$, so (T) gives $p^w_c+1=\tilde t_A$, that is, $p^w_c=\omega-3r<\mu_w$, which is impossible. If $t^z_A$ takes its lower bound and the event is $t^w_A$, then det holds, and as above $t^z_A=\zeta-3r$ if $\zeta-3r<1$ and $t^z_A\ge1$ if $\zeta-3r=1$. In the first case $\bar x_A=\frac13(1+r+\omega)$. Then $3r\le\bar x_A+2\bar x_B$ gives $8r\le4+4\omega\le0$. In the second case $\bar x_A\le0$ and $\bar x_B=\frac12(1+\omega)=-\frac12r$. Then $3r\le\bar x_A+2\bar x_B$ gives $4r\le\bar x_A\le0$. Both contradict $r>0$.

(b) By Proposition~\ref{prop:d5zero}(d), $r=0$, and one of $f_A$, $f_B$ is equal to $\mu_w\le-1$. By (Q) and (R), $\tau_A=\tau_B$ and $\tau_X\ge-\bar x_X$, with equality unless $\tau_X$ is the event of $X$. Suppose that $f_B<f_A$. Then $\tau_A=\tau_B\ge-\bar x_B>-\bar x_A$. So $\tau_A$ is the event of $A$. Hence $c_A=1$ and $t^z_A$, $t^w_A$ take their lower bounds. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(a), $f_B=\omega=-\zeta$ and $\mu_z=1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_A\ge1$, that is, $f_A\le-1$. If $\zeta>1$, then $\zeta$ is the exception in $z$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:d5rules}(b) gives $t^z_A=t^z_B=1$. So $f_A=-1$. Then $t^z_B=1\ge-\frac12(1+3f_B)$ contradicts $f_B<-1$. If $\zeta=1$, then $f_B=-1<f_A\le-1$. By symmetry $f_A=f_B$ and both are equal to $\mu_w\le-1$, that is, $\bar x_A=\bar x_B\le0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:d5sym} it suffices to treat the nine pairs of Table~\ref{tab:d5hulls}. Proposition~\ref{prop:d5empty} gives the empty pairs. For (Z1,\,W1), (F,\,F), (F,\,Z1) and (Z1,\,Z1), Proposition~\ref{prop:d5zero} gives $y=\bar x_Ae_A+\bar x_Be_B$ with the stated conditions, and $\bar x_A,\bar x_B\in[-\frac12,1]$; these points lie in the polytopes of the table. For (Zs,\,Zs), Proposition~\ref{prop:d5ss} gives $y\in\mathcal R\cup\mathcal T$. For (Z1,\,Zs), Proposition~\ref{prop:d5zs} gives $y\in\mathcal S^0\cup\mathcal S^+\cup\mathcal S^-$. Proposition~\ref{prop:d5VN} gives the column of $V_N$ and the centred case; for (F,\,F) and (Zs,\,Zs) the model of $V_N$ lies in that of $V_2$. We find the vertices of $\mathcal R$, $\mathcal S^0$, $\mathcal S^+$ and $\mathcal S^-$ by the following remark. Let $\Delta$ be a polytope and $q_1,\dots,q_k$ affine maps on $\Delta$. If $\delta=\sum_v\lambda_vv$ is a convex combination of the vertices $v$ of $\Delta$ and $u=\sum_j\mu_jq_j(\delta)$ is a convex combination, then $(\delta,u)=\sum_{v,j}\lambda_v\mu_j\,(v,q_j(v))$. So every point $(\delta,u)$ with $\delta\in\Delta$ and $u\in\operatorname{conv}\{q_1(\delta),\dots,q_k(\delta)\}$ lies in the convex hull of the points $(v,q_j(v))$.

On $\{y_5=0\}$ we put $u_1=y_1+2y_2$ and $u_2=y_3+2y_4$. Since $y_2\le y_1\le0$ means $3y_2\le u_1\le2y_2$, and likewise for $y_3$ and $y_4$, the polytope $\mathcal R$ is the set of the points with $y_2,y_4\ge-\frac12$ and $3\max(y_2,y_4)\le u_1,u_2\le2\min(y_2,y_4)$. Over the triangle $-\frac12\le y_2\le y_4\le\frac23y_2$, with the vertices $(y_2,y_4)=(-\frac12,-\frac12)$, $(-\frac12,-\frac13)$ and $(0,0)$, the bounds are $3y_4$ and $2y_2$, and $(u_1,u_2)$ lies in the square spanned by the four pairs of bounds; over the triangle with $y_2$ and $y_4$ exchanged the same holds. By the remark, $\mathcal R$ lies in the convex hull of the points with $(y_2,y_4)=(-\frac12,-\frac12)$ and $u_1,u_2\in\{-\frac32,-1\}$, the points with $(y_2,y_4)=(-\frac12,-\frac13)$ or $(-\frac13,-\frac12)$ and $u_1=u_2=-1$, and $0$. These seven points lie in $\mathcal R$. They are the seven vertices of $P_{ss}$ with $y_5=0$. The triangle $\mathcal T$ is the convex hull of two of them and $(\frac13,0,\frac13,0,\frac13)$. So $P_{ss}=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal R\cup\mathcal T)$, a pyramid over $\mathcal R$ with apex $(\frac13,0,\frac13,0,\frac13)$.

The points of $\mathcal S^0$, $\mathcal S^+$ and $\mathcal S^-$ have $y_1=y_2$ and $-\frac12\le y_4\le0$. They are determined by $y_4$ and the pair $(y_1,y_3)$, $(y_1,y_5)$, resp.\ $(y_1,y_5)$. For fixed $y_4$ this pair ranges over the rectangle $[y_4,1]\times[y_4,0]$ for $\mathcal S^0$ (where $y_5=0$), over the triangle with the vertices $(-2y_4,0)$, $(1,0)$ and $(1,\frac13(1+2y_4))$ for $\mathcal S^+$ (where $y_3=y_5$), and over the rectangle $[-2y_4,1]\times[y_4,0]$ for $\mathcal S^-$ (where $y_3=0$). By the remark, applied over the segment $-\frac12\le y_4\le0$, $\mathcal S^0$ lies in the convex hull of $-\frac12(e_A+e_B)$, $(-\frac12,-\frac12,0,-\frac12,0)$, $0$, $e_A-\frac12e_B$, $(1,1,0,-\frac12,0)$ and $e_A$, $\mathcal S^+$ in that of $0$, $(1,1,0,-\frac12,0)$, $e_A$ and $(1,1,\frac13,0,\frac13)$, and $\mathcal S^-$ in that of $0$, $(1,1,0,-\frac12,-\frac12)$, $(1,1,0,-\frac12,0)$ and $e_A$. These points lie in the respective sets. Together they are the eight vertices of $P_{1s}$. So $P_{1s}=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal S^0\cup\mathcal S^+\cup\mathcal S^-)$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d2branch}
After a rotation depending on the local parameter and a change of the parameter, the coordinates near $P$ are $q=T^{w_q}y_q(\xi)$ with $T=\xi^L$ for an integer $L\ge1$, where the $y_q$ are convergent power series in $\xi$ with $y_{u_1}\equiv y_{v_1}\equiv1$, $G(\xi^L,y(\xi))\equiv0$, and $y(0)$ is a leading solution.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{lem:place}, after the rotation there, each coordinate is $\vartheta^{d\,e_q}\tilde y_q(\vartheta)$ with $\tilde y_q(0)\ne0$. We put $L=2d$ (a positive integer) and $T=\vartheta^L$, so that $q=T^{w_q}\tilde y_q$. A further rotation by the unit $\tilde y_{u_1}^{-1}$ makes $y_{u_1}\equiv1$ and multiplies all other $\tilde y_q$ by units. The zero set of $G_0$ is invariant under $y_q\mapsto\lambda^{e'_q}y_q$, with $e'_q=w_q-w_{u_1}$, $w_q+w_{u_1}$ or $w_q$ for $q$ a $u_k$, a $v_k$ or a $p_{kl}$, which comes from $T\mapsto\lambda T$ combined with a rotation. In particular, $e'_{u_1}=0$ and $e'_{v_1}=-2$. Replacing $T$ by $T'\phi^L$ and rotating accordingly turns $y_q$ into $\phi^{Le'_q}y_q$. The equation $\phi^{-2L}y_{v_1}(\xi\phi)=1$ is solved by a convergent $\phi(\xi)$, $\phi(0)^{2L}=y_{v_1}(0)$, by the implicit function theorem. Since all rows vanish on $X_m$, $G(\xi^L,y(\xi))\equiv0$. At $\xi=0$ this gives $G_0(y(0))=0$.

body_md:
\label{lem:d2lead}
At a leading solution: $u_2=-m_1/m_2$, $p_{12}^3=1/(m_1+m_2)$, $v_2=v_c:=(m_3v_3+m_4v_4)/M_t=1$; with $\omega_k=v_k-v_c$ for $k\in\{3,4,5\}$ (so $\omega_5=-1$ and $\sum_km_k\omega_k=0$), $p_{1k}^2=-1/\omega_k$ and $p_{2k}=\sigma_k\mathrm{j}_\rho p_{1k}$ with $\sigma_k=\pm1$; and the triangle coordinates $u_3,u_4,v_3,v_4,p_{34},p_{35},p_{45}$ satisfy $F'_3=F'_4=F'_5$ for $h=u$ and for $h=v$ and $p_{kl}^2u_{kl}v_{kl}=1$, so they form a complex central configuration of three bodies: of Lagrange type ($p_{kl}^3=1/M_t$) or of Euler type ($u$ parallel to $v$).

title: Proof
body_md: The least-weight parts of $Z_1$, $Z_2$ are $u_1-m_2p_{12}^3(u_1-u_2)$ and its mirror, which give $u_2$ and $p_{12}$. That of $D_{12}$ gives $v_2=v_1=1$. Those of $W_1$ and of $m_3W_3+m_4W_4$ give $v_2=\bar v$ and $\bar v=v_c$, where $\bar v=m_3v_3p_{35}^3+m_4v_4p_{45}^3$. Those of $D_{1k}$, $D_{2k}$ are $p_{1k}^2(1-v_k)-1$ and $p_{2k}^2u_2(1-v_k)-1$. The remaining seven rows are the three-body rows of the triangle. For the dichotomy let $\Psi(h)_k=\sum_lm_lp_{kl}^3(h_k-h_l)$. By antisymmetry $\Psi$ maps the plane $\sum_km_kh_k=0$ to itself. The vectors $u-u_{\mathrm{cm}}\mathbb{1}$ and $\omega$ are fixed vectors of $\Psi$ in it. If they are independent, $\Psi$ is the identity on the plane, and comparing the quadratic forms $\sum_km_kh_k\Psi(h)_k$ and $\sum_km_kh_k^2$, we obtain $p_{kl}^3=1/M_t$. Otherwise $\omega$ is a multiple of $u-u_{\mathrm{cm}}\mathbb{1}$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d2rot}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $\ell(y)\cdot G_0(y)=0$ identically.
\item $G_1$ vanishes on every row except $Z_3$, $Z_4$, where $G_{1,Z_k}=\sum_{j=1,2}m_ju_j(p_{kj}^3-p_{5j}^3)$. Moreover, $\ell\cdot G_2\equiv0$ and $\ell\cdot G_n\equiv0$ for $n\ge4$.
\item At a leading solution, $G_{1,Z_k}=-(\theta_k-\theta_5)$ and $\tau=-M_t\sum_{k\in\{3,4,5\}}\tau_k$.
\item $\ell(y)\cdot G(T,y)=T\tau(y)+T^3\sigma_3(y)$, so along the series of Lemma~\ref{lem:d2branch}, $\tau(y(\xi))=-T^2\sigma_3(y(\xi))$. In particular $\tau(y_0)=0$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md: (a) The rows $Z_k$, $W_k$ of $G_0$, $k\in\{3,4\}$, are $F'_k-F'_5$ at $u$ and at $v$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:d2lead}). By antisymmetry $\sum_km_kF'_k(u)=s_u$, $\sum_km_kF'_k(v)=s_v$ and $\sum_km_k\big(v_kF'_k(u)-u_kF'_k(v)\big)=0$. Inserting these into $\ell\cdot G_0$ gives $0$. Note that this is the conservation of angular momentum of the triangle. (b) Each row is a polynomial in $T$. In $Z_k$, $k\in\{3,4\}$, the terms with a factor $p_{kj}$ or $p_{5j}$, $j\in\{1,2\}$, have weight $2$ (those with $u_j$) or $4$, one or three more than the least weight $1$. Hence $Z_k$ has only the relative exponents $0$, $1$, $3$. In $W_k$ these terms have weight $2$, three more than $-1$. So $W_k$ has only $0$ and $3$. The other rows have the relative exponents $0$, $2$, $3$ and $5$ ($Z_1$, $Z_2$), $0$ and $3$ ($W_1$, $W_2$), $0$ and $2$ ($D_{12}$ and $D_{jk}$, $j\in\{1,2\}$, $k\in\{3,4\}$) and $0$ ($D_{15}$, $D_{25}$ and the sides of the triangle). Since $\ell$ is supported on $Z_3,Z_4,W_3,W_4$, the coefficients of $T^2$ and of $T^n$, $n\ge4$, vanish there. label: lem:d2simple
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d2simple}
Let $y_0$ be a leading solution with $\tau(y_0)=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}J_0=16$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item The left kernel of $J_0$ is spanned by $\lambda$ and $l_0=e_{W_1}-e_{W_2}$, and $J_0y_1=-G_1(y_0)$ has exactly one solution $y_1$.
\item $y_1$ vanishes on $u_2,p_{12},v_2$; $(y_1)_{p_{jk}}=-p_{jk}(y_1)_{v_k}/(2\omega_k)$ for $j\in\{1,2\}$, $k\in\{3,4\}$, and $(y_1)_{p_{j5}}=0$; and $m_3(y_1)_{v_3}+m_4(y_1)_{v_4}=0$. Write $(y_1)_{v_3}=t/m_3$, $(y_1)_{v_4}=-t/m_4$.
\item A series as in Lemma~\ref{lem:d2branch} with $y(0)=y_0$ exists only if
\[
\eta_2:=D\tau(y_0)\cdot y_1=\tfrac12M_t\,t\,(\theta_3-\theta_4)=0 .
\]
\item Suppose that $\theta$ is constant. Then $y_1=0$, and, with $y_2$ the solution of $J_0y_2=-G_2(y_0)$, a series as in \textup{(c)} exists only if
\[
\Omega_3:=\lambda\cdot\big(DG_1(y_0)\,y_2+G_3(y_0)\big)=D\tau(y_0)\cdot y_2+\sigma_3(y_0)=0 .
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) $\lambda J_0=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:d2rot}(a), and $l_0J_0=0$ because the rows $W_1$, $W_2$ of $G_0$ differ by $(1-v_2)(1-(m_1+m_2)p_{12}^3)$, whose gradient vanishes at a leading solution. The two vectors are independent ($\lambda_{Z_k}=M_tm_k\omega_k\ne0$). Thus they span the left kernel, of dimension $2$. Since $\lambda\cdot G_1=\tau=0$ and $l_0\cdot G_1=0$, a solution $y_1$ exists. It is unique by the rank.
(b) The rows $Z_1$, $Z_2$, $D_{12}$ of $G_0$ involve only $u_2,p_{12},v_2$, with an invertible Jacobian there, and zero right side. The rows $D_{jk}$ give the across entries. The row $W_1$ and the identity $m_3W_3+m_4W_4=s_v-M_t\bar v$ of the rows of $G_0$ give $D s_v\cdot y_1=0$.
(c) Since $J_0$ is injective, the series is a power series in $T$ with first coefficient $y_1$ (the coefficient of a non-integral power, if any, would be in the kernel of $J_0$). So $\tau(y(T))=T\,D\tau(y_0)y_1+O(T^2)$, which is $O(T^2)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:d2rot}(d). For the formula: $\tau=\sum_{k=3,4}\ell_{Z_k}G_{1,Z_k}$. By (b), $DG_{1,Z_k}\cdot y_1=\frac{3(y_1)_{v_k}}{2\omega_k}\theta_k$ and $D\omega_k\cdot y_1=(y_1)_{v_k}$. Hence we obtain $D\tau\cdot y_1=M_t\sum_{k=3,4}m_k\big(-(\theta_k-\theta_5)+\frac32\theta_k\big)(y_1)_{v_k}=\frac12M_t\sum_{k=3,4}m_k\theta_k(y_1)_{v_k}$, using $\sum_{k=3,4}m_k(y_1)_{v_k}=0$.
(d) Since $G_1(y_0)=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:d2theta}, $y_1=0$. The equation at order $T^2$ is solvable because $\lambda\cdot G_2\equiv0$ and $G_2$ vanishes on the rows $W$. At order $T^3$ the equation is $J_0y_3=-(DG_1(y_0)y_2+G_3(y_0))$. Its $l_0$-component vanishes (it is the cross part of $F'_1(v)-F'_2(v)$, a multiple of $\tau$). Its $\lambda$-component is $\Omega_3$. The second expression for $\Omega_3$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:d2rot}(d).

label: lem:d2forcing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d2forcing}
There is a number $\gamma$ with $\theta-\bar\theta\mathbb{1}=\gamma e_3$. Moreover $\theta_3-\theta_4=-\gamma M_t\omega_5/(m_3m_4)$, and $\gamma=0$ if and only if $\theta$ is constant.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{lem:d2rot}(c), $\langle\omega,\theta\rangle=\sum_k\tau_k=-\tau/M_t=0$. So $\psi=\theta-\bar\theta\mathbb{1}$ satisfies $\langle\mathbb{1},\psi\rangle=\langle\omega,\psi\rangle=0$. Since $\langle\mathbb{1},\omega\rangle=0$ and $\omega_5=-1$, $\omega$ is not a multiple of $\mathbb{1}$. Hence these two conditions define a line. It contains $e_3\ne0$. The formula for $\theta_3-\theta_4$ follows from $m_4v_{45}-m_3v_{53}=m_3\omega_3+m_4\omega_4-(m_3+m_4)\omega_5=-M_t\omega_5$. Finally $\gamma=0$ if and only if $\psi=0$.

label: thm:d2closed
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:d2closed}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item Let the triangle be of Lagrange type, and let $y_0$ not be a triple point. Put $r_{kl}=u_{kl}/v_{kl}$, $\beta=m_5r_{34}+m_4r_{35}+m_3r_{45}$, $\Delta=u_{34}v_{35}-u_{35}v_{34}$ and $d_r=(r_{34}-r_{35})/m_3+(r_{34}-r_{45})/m_4$. Then $\Delta\ne0$, $d_r\ne0$, $y_0$ is simple, and
\[
\eta_2=-\gamma^2\,\frac{M_t^3\,\omega_5\,v_{34}v_{35}v_{45}\,\beta}{3\,\Delta\,d_r\,m_3^2m_4^2m_5}.
\]
\item Let the triangle be of Euler type, $u=\Lambda v$, with $\langle\omega,\omega\rangle\ne0$, and put $\mu=\sum_{k<l}(m_k+m_l)P_{kl}-1$. If $\mu=1$, then $y_0$ is a triple point. If $\mu\notin\{1,-\frac12\}$, then $y_0$ is simple, and
\[
\eta_2=-\gamma^2\,\frac{3M_t\,\mu\,\langle e_3,e_3\rangle}{4\Lambda(1-\mu)(1+2\mu)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $J_T$ be the triangle block of $J_0$. It has the rows $Z_3,Z_4,W_3,W_4,D_{34},D_{35},D_{45}$ and the columns of $u_3,u_4,v_3,v_4,p_{34},p_{35},p_{45}$. These rows of $G_0$ contain no other coordinates (Lemma~\ref{lem:d2lead}). For a vector $x$ in these columns we write $\delta$ for the derivative along $x$. Then $J_Tx=0$ says that $\delta F'_k(u)$ and $\delta F'_k(v)$ do not depend on $k\in\{3,4,5\}$ and that $\delta P_{kl}/P_{kl}=-\frac32(\delta u_{kl}/u_{kl}+\delta v_{kl}/v_{kl})$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d2rot}(c), the triangle part of $y_1$ satisfies the same conditions with $\delta F'_k(u)-\theta_k$ in place of $\delta F'_k(u)$. The rotation $R$, with $\delta u_k=u_k$, $\delta v_k=-v_k$ and $\delta p=0$, lies in $\ker J_T$, since the rows are invariant under $(u,v)\mapsto(\alpha u,\alpha^{-1}v)$. If $\ker J_T=\mathbb{C} R$, then $y_0$ is simple. Indeed, let $J_0x=0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d2simple}(b) holds for $x$ with zero right sides. So the triangle part of $x$ is $cR$ for a number $c$, and $0=m_3\delta v_3+m_4\delta v_4=-c(m_3v_3+m_4v_4)=-cM_t$. Hence $c=0$, and then $x=0$.

(a) Here $P_{kl}=1/M_t$, so that $\delta F'_k(h)=\langle\mathbb{1},\delta h\rangle/M_t-\sum_lm_lh_{kl}\delta P_{kl}$ for $h=u,v$. Since $\sum_km_k\sum_lm_lh_{kl}\delta P_{kl}=0$, the triangle part of $y_1$ satisfies $\sum_lm_lv_{kl}\delta P_{kl}=0$ and $\sum_lm_lu_{kl}\delta P_{kl}=\bar\theta-\theta_k$ for $k\in\{3,4,5\}$. A vector of $\ker J_T$ satisfies the same equations with $0$ in place of $\bar\theta-\theta_k$. The equations in $v$ have rank $2$ and give $\delta P=\kappa_L\delta^0$ with $\delta^0=(m_5v_{35}v_{45},-m_4v_{34}v_{45},m_3v_{34}v_{35})$ on $(34,35,45)$. The equation in $u$ for $k=3$ then reads $\kappa_Lm_4m_5v_{45}\Delta=\bar\theta-\theta_3$. Here $\Delta\ne0$. Otherwise $(u_{34},u_{35})$ is a multiple of $(v_{34},v_{35})$, so that $u$ is parallel to $v$ and $y_0$ is a triple point. The rows $D_{kl}$ give $\delta u_{kl}=-\frac23M_tu_{kl}\delta P_{kl}-r_{kl}\delta v_{kl}$. We sum over the cycle $34,45,53$ and put $\phi(\delta v)=(r_{34}-r_{35})\delta v_3+(r_{45}-r_{34})\delta v_4$. This gives $\phi(\delta v)=-\frac23M_t\kappa_Lv_{34}v_{35}v_{45}\beta$. The linear form $\phi$ vanishes at $(v_3,v_4)$. It is not zero, since otherwise $r_{34}=r_{35}=r_{45}$ and $y_0$ is a triple point.

For a vector of $\ker J_T$ we obtain $\kappa_L=0$ and $\delta P=0$, and then $\phi(\delta v)=0$. So $\delta v$ is a multiple $cv$ of $v$, $\delta u_{kl}=-r_{kl}\delta v_{kl}=-cu_{kl}$, and the vector lies in $\mathbb{C} R$. Thus $y_0$ is simple. Next, $d_r=\phi(1/m_3,-1/m_4)$. The vector $(1/m_3,-1/m_4)$ is not a multiple of $(v_3,v_4)$, since $m_3v_3+m_4v_4=M_t\ne0$. Hence $d_r\ne0$. For $y_1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d2simple}(b) gives $\delta v_3=t/m_3$ and $\delta v_4=-t/m_4$, so that $\phi(\delta v)=t\,d_r$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d2forcing} gives $\bar\theta-\theta_3=-\gamma v_{45}/m_3$, hence $\kappa_L=-\gamma/(m_3m_4m_5\Delta)$ and
\[
t=\frac{2M_t\gamma\,v_{34}v_{35}v_{45}\,\beta}{3m_3m_4m_5\Delta\,d_r}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:d2simple}(c) and the formula for $\theta_3-\theta_4$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:d2forcing} give the formula for $\eta_2$.

(b) We write $\delta u=\Lambda(\delta v+\varepsilon)$ on the triangle, with $\varepsilon_5=0$. Then $\delta P_{kl}/P_{kl}=-3\delta v_{kl}/v_{kl}-\frac32\varepsilon_{kl}/v_{kl}$. With $\Psi(h)_k=\sum_lm_lP_{kl}(h_k-h_l)$ as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:d2lead} we obtain
\[
\delta F'(v)=(1+2\Psi)\delta v+\tfrac32\Psi\varepsilon,\qquad\delta F'(u)=\Lambda\big(\delta F'(v)+(1-\Psi)\varepsilon\big).
\]
The map $\Psi$ is self-adjoint for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $\Psi\mathbb{1}=0$, and $\Psi\omega=\omega$ by the rows of $v$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:d2lead}. Since $\langle\mathbb{1},\mathbb{1}\rangle=M_t$, $\langle\mathbb{1},\omega\rangle=0$ and $\langle\omega,\omega\rangle\ne0$, the vectors $\mathbb{1}$, $\omega$, $e_3$ form a basis, and $\Psi e_3=\mu'e_3$ for a number $\mu'$. The trace of $\Psi$ is $\sum_{k<l}(m_k+m_l)P_{kl}=1+\mu'$. So $\mu'=\mu$.

If $\mu=1$, then $\Psi$ agrees on this basis with the map $h\mapsto h-\langle\mathbb{1},h\rangle\mathbb{1}/M_t$. Comparing the entries off the diagonal gives $P_{kl}=1/M_t$. So the triangle is also of Lagrange type, and $y_0$ is a triple point.

Let $\mu\notin\{1,-\frac12\}$. For a vector of $\ker J_T$, both $\Lambda(1-\Psi)\varepsilon=\delta F'(u)-\Lambda\,\delta F'(v)$ and $\delta F'(v)$ are multiples of $\mathbb{1}$. In the basis $\mathbb{1},\omega,e_3$ this puts $\varepsilon$ and $\delta v$ into $\mathbb{C}\mathbb{1}+\mathbb{C}\omega$. Since $\varepsilon_5=\delta v_5=0$ and $v=\mathbb{1}+\omega$, both are multiples of $v$. The equation for $\delta F'(v)$ then gives $\varepsilon=-2\,\delta v$. Thus $\delta u=-\Lambda\,\delta v$ and $\delta P=0$, and the vector lies in $\mathbb{C} R$. So $y_0$ is simple. For $y_1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:d2forcing} gives $\theta=\bar\theta\mathbb{1}+\gamma e_3$. In the basis $\mathbb{1},\omega,e_3$ the coefficient of $e_3$ is $\gamma/(\Lambda(1-\mu))$ in $\varepsilon$ and $-\frac32\mu\gamma/(\Lambda(1-\mu)(1+2\mu))$ in $\delta v$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:d2simple}(b), $\delta v=(t/m_3,-t/m_4,0)$. So $\langle\mathbb{1},\delta v\rangle=0$, and $t(\theta_3-\theta_4)=\langle\theta,\delta v\rangle=\gamma\langle e_3,\delta v\rangle$. This is $\gamma\langle e_3,e_3\rangle$ times the coefficient of $e_3$ in $\delta v$. Lemma~\ref{lem:d2simple}(c) gives the formula for $\eta_2$.

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) For equal $\zeta_{kl}$ the quadratic is $\chi^2-\chi+1$, whose roots are $e^{\pm i\pi/3}$. For $(\zeta_{34},\zeta_{35},\zeta_{45})=(\varpi^2,\varpi,1)$ and $(1,\varpi,\varpi^2)$ it is $(\chi+\varpi^2)^2$, resp.\ $\varpi^2(\chi+\varpi)^2$. Every class with distinct $\zeta_{kl}$ is a multiple of one of these two. The double root gives an equilateral triangle with $v_{kl}^2$ proportional to $\zeta_{kl}$. Then $r_{kl}=M_t^{2/3}\zeta_{kl}/v_{kl}^2$ does not depend on $kl$, so that $u$ is parallel to $v$. Let exactly two of the $\zeta_{kl}$ be equal. Complex conjugation conjugates the class and the shape, and a relabelling of the triangle permutes the masses. These maps reduce the claims to the class $(\zeta_{34},\zeta_{35},\zeta_{45})=(1,1,\varpi)$. There $\chi^2-\chi+\varpi^2=0$. So $\chi$ is not real, and $\operatorname{Re}\chi=\frac12\big(1\pm((3+\sqrt{21})/2)^{1/2}\big)$ is $1.47\ldots$ or $-0.47\ldots$. Hence the triangle $\chi,1,0$ is obtuse at $1$ or at $0$.

(b) As in (a) we take the class $(1,1,\varpi)$. There $\chi^2(\chi-1)^2=\varpi$, and $\beta=0$ reads $m_3+m_4/\eta+m_5\eta=0$ with $\eta=\varpi\chi^2$. Since $\chi=\varpi^2(\eta+1)$, we get $\eta^2+(2-\varpi)\eta+1=0$, and $\eta$ is not real. Hence $\eta$ and $\bar\eta$ are the roots of $m_5T^2+m_3T+m_4$, so that $m_4/m_5=|\eta|^2$ and $m_3/m_5=-2\operatorname{Re}\eta$. The two roots $\eta$ and $1/\eta$ give mass vectors that differ by the exchange of $m_4$ and $m_5$. Moreover $|\eta|\ne1$, since $\eta+1/\eta$ is not real. For the root with $t=|\eta|^2>1$ we write $\eta=a+bi$. Then $\eta+1/\eta=\varpi-2$ gives $a(1+t^{-1})=-\frac52$ and $b(1-t^{-1})=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, and $a^2+b^2=t$ becomes $t^4-7t^3+9t^2-7t+1=0$. So $t+t^{-1}$ is a root of $s^2-7s+7$. It is $(7+\sqrt{21})/2$, since the other root is less than $2$. Thus $(m_3:m_4:m_5)=(5t/(t+1):t:1)=(Y_L:1:X_L)$ with $X_L=1/t$ and $Y_L=5/(t+1)$.

(c) If $\theta$ is constant, the moduli $|\omega_k|$ are equal (\S\ref{ss:d2torque}). Then the centre of mass of the triangle $v_3,v_4,v_5$ in $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}^2$ is its circumcentre. With positive masses it lies inside the triangle, which is therefore acute. This contradicts (a).
